docs.text:
Info

This website offers a full functional analysis of the project. Based on the Archiku Analysis MetaModel, it organises each finding as a connected fact.

Several reports provide combined views of the facts, while every fact appears as a linked page. This forms a wiki-like setting, enabling you to move through the codebase by meaning and function.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
It is a household ledger — the archetype story calls it a double-entry-adjacent personal ledger with a forecast layer — and its whole design protects one thing: books that can prove their own history.

  1. The books replay their own history: every change joins an append-only, content-hashed journal — timestamped so even identical same-day recordings stay distinct — and every row re-verifies on read; a correction is a new recorded event, never a quiet edit.
  2. Planned money cannot corrupt recorded money: recurring rules and their forecast are an overlay never materialized into the books, and the only bridge from plan to reality is the deliberately zero-prompt confirm of a landed entry.
  3. A caution for bulk-cleanup reviews: an amount correction on a transfer row silently overwrites any custom savings side — a reviewer fixing one field should expect both sides to rewrite.
  4. Destructive actions demand a typed affirmative and offer no undo; the journal — not a restore command — is the recovery story.

Verification status: no objection facts and no verification-phase records exist in the fact base at narration time, so these findings rest on the analyst passes' own confidence.

Next step: read the companion product summary and archetype mapping for the capability walk and concept map, then the per-surface detail sections.

Read the full functional analysis report...

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A shorthand's "Head: rest" form reads its head as a category only when it resolves to the household's approved vocabulary — the alias rule decides what becomes a category.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Not a party in the usual sense but the vocabulary role the parser assigns: when a quick-add line carries "Word: text", that Word is treated as a category candidate only if it canonicalizes against the approved set. When it does not, the whole text stays description. The alias rule is the parser's guard against description text being swallowed as a category by accident — the def teaches the party identity law, and while this is a role the process recognizes, its capture here keeps the vocabulary story complete. The pool/one-part law does not require this in the script: the intake's category question covers it.

def _canonical_category(text: str) -> str | None:
  lowered = text.strip().lower()
  for approved in approved_categories():
    if approved.lower() == lowered:
      return approved
  return None

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The party who authors and reviews the cleanup change-set files — historical-mistake corrections prepared offline and then applied by the tool in bulk.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The reviewer works upstream of the tool: they identify historical mistakes (wrong categories or amounts recorded by an older process), write each correction as one fix naming its target row, optionally state the value they saw to guard against drift, and give each change a reason. Their review is the tool's authority: the engine trusts a file it is pointed at and refuses only on hard guards. They also own recovery — when a change-set fails partway, deciding whether to repair or drop the remainder is theirs. Their stake is that the correction lands exactly as reviewed, on the rows they named, with nothing applied that their review did not approve.

def _load_fixes_file(fixes_path: Path) -> list[dict]:
  """Load a fixes file; format follows the extension (.json or .toml).
  TOML arrays of tables ([[fixes]]) are the preferred, readable format."""
  if fixes_path.suffix == ".toml":
    import tomllib

    with open(fixes_path, "rb") as fh:
      document = tomllib.load(fh)
    return document.get("fixes", [])
  with open(fixes_path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    document = json.load(fh)
  return document.get("fixes", [])

# src/financials/fixes.py — lines 257–267
def apply_fixes(fixes_path: Path) -> None:
  """Apply a hand-authored fixes file against the journaled ledger:
  field ops route to apply_field_ops (one UpdateMutation each), row ops
  (remove_row/add_expected_row) route through apply_ops."""
  fixes = _load_fixes_file(fixes_path)
  field_fixes = [fix for fix in fixes if "field" in fix]
  row_fixes = [fix for fix in fixes if "field" not in fix]
  if field_fixes:
    apply_field_ops(field_fixes, source=fixes_path.name)
  if row_fixes:
    apply_ops(row_fixes, source=fixes_path.name)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The person keeping the household's cashflow recorded — spends and income go through their add session the moment they remember it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The household bookkeeper is the process's single business participant. When a spend or income happens (or is remembered), they open the add surface and record it — either as a one-line quick-add shorthand ("gisteren -25 Kafe") or by answering the step-by-step prompts. They are asked for anything the shorthand or flags omit; nothing is silently assumed, and a confirmation prompt shows the projected checking balance before they accept. If they type a future-dated movement, it is parked as a plan in the expected register instead of entering the actual books. Their interest: a permanently recorded transaction that carries a correct running balance, and the ability to abort without leaving a trace when the session reveals a mistake.

# src/financials/entry.py — lines 94–178
def _prompt(
  ledger: Ledger,
  seed: Shorthand | None = None,
) -> tuple[str, str, str, float, float | None] | None:
  """Interactive prompt loop. Returns entry values, or None on abort.
  `seed` pre-fills prompts from a parsed quick-add shorthand."""
  from financials.entry import _chain_last_entry

  last = _chain_last_entry(ledger)

  console.print(
    "[bold]Nieuwe transactie[/bold] [dim](leeg antwoord = standaardwaarde, 'q' = annuleren)[/dim]"
  )
  if last is not None:
    checking = last.balances.get("checking")
    savings = last.balances.get("savings")
    console.print(
      f"[dim]Laatste rij: {last.date.isoformat()} {last.description} — checking "
      f"{checking:,.2f}, spaar {savings:,.2f}[/dim]"
    )
    if date.today().isoformat() < last.date.isoformat():
      console.print(
        "[yellow]Let op: de laatste rij ligt in de toekomst; kies een datum "
        "erna om de balansen te kunnen doorzetten.[/yellow]"
      )

  last_date = last.date.isoformat() if last is not None else ""
  default_date = seed.date if seed and seed.date else max(date.today().isoformat(), last_date)
  iso_date = Prompt.ask("Datum (YYYY-MM-DD)", default=default_date)
  if iso_date == "q":
    return None
  try:
    is_future = date.fromisoformat(iso_date) > date.today()
  except ValueError:
    is_future = False  # invalid format: let _validate produce the error
  if is_future:
    console.print(
      "[dim]Toekomstige datum — opgeslagen in het expected-register (geen saldo-doorvoer).[/dim]"
    )
  description = Prompt.ask(
    "Omschrijving", default=(seed.description if seed and seed.description else "")
  )
  if description == "q":
    return None
  category = ask_category(current=(seed.category if seed and seed.category else ""))
  if category == ABORT or category is None:
    return None
  amount: float
  if seed and seed.amount is not None:
    amount = seed.amount
  else:
    amount_text = Prompt.ask("Bedrag (positief = inkomsten, negatief = uitgaven, bv. -38.93)")
    if amount_text == "q":
      return None
    parsed = _validate_amount(amount_text)
    if parsed is None:
      console.print("[red]Ongeldig bedrag (0 is niet toegelaten).[/red]")
      return None
    amount = parsed

  # Project from the ledger's date-positioned predecessor of the typed
  # date — the same row the engine will chain from.
  if not is_future:
    projected, predecessor = projected_checking(ledger, iso_date, amount)
    if projected is not None and predecessor is not None:
      console.print(f"[dim]Geprojecteerd checking-saldo: {projected:,.2f}[/dim]")
      for attempt in range(1, RETRY_LIMIT + 1):
        checking_text = Prompt.ask(
          "Nieuw checking-saldo (leeg = geprojecteerd)", default=f"{projected:.2f}"
        )
        if checking_text == "q":
          return None
        try:
          checking = round(float(checking_text.replace(",", ".")), 2)
        except ValueError:
          console.print("[red]Ongeldig saldo.[/red]")
          continue
        if abs(checking - projected) < 0.005:
          return iso_date, description, category, amount, checking
        console.print(
          f"[red]Komt niet overeen met {projected:,.2f} (poging {attempt}/{RETRY_LIMIT}).[/red]"
        )
      console.print("[red]Te vaak mislukt — geannuleerd.[/red]")
      return None
  return iso_date, description, category, amount, None

# src/financials/entry.py — lines 181–287
def add_transaction(
  iso_date: str | None = None,
  description: str | None = None,
  category: str | None = None,
  amount: float | None = None,
  checking: float | None = None,
  dry_run: bool = False,
  shorthand: str | None = None,
  journal: Journal | None = None,
) -> int:
  """Add a transaction. Three paths:
  - fully flagged: validates and appends directly;
  - shorthand: "gisteren -25 Kafe" pre-seeds the interactive prompts
    (anything the shorthand omits is asked, Enter accepts the seed);
  - bare: fully interactive.
  Returns 0 on success, 2 on rejection/abort."""
  ledger = _boot(journal)
  seed: Shorthand | None = None
  if shorthand:
    try:
      seed = parse_shorthand(shorthand)
    except ShorthandError as exc:
      console.print(f"[red]Niet opgeslagen: {exc}[/red]")
      return 2
    console.print(
      f"[dim]Shorthand: {seed.date or '(datum gevraagd)'}  "
      f"{seed.category or '(categorie gevraagd)'}  "
      f"{seed.description or '(omschrijving gevraagd)'}  "
      f"{seed.amount if seed.amount is not None else '(bedrag gevraagd)'}[/dim]"
    )
    iso_date = iso_date if iso_date is not None else seed.date
    description = description if description is not None else seed.description
    category = category if category is not None else seed.category
    amount = amount if amount is not None else seed.amount
  if (
    iso_date is not None
    and description is not None
    and category is not None
    and amount is not None
    and iso_date > date.today().isoformat()
  ):
    # Date-based dispatch: future → expected register (fully-specified
    # flag/shorthand path; partial values fall through to the prompts,
    # whose dispatch handles the future case once all fields are known).
    console.print("[dim]→ expected-register (financials expect).[/dim]")
    return add_expected(
      iso_date=iso_date,
      description=description,
      category=category,
      amount=amount,
      dry_run=dry_run,
    )
  if iso_date is None or description is None or category is None or amount is None:
    prompted = _prompt(
      ledger,
      seed=seed
      if (iso_date is None or description is None or category is None or amount is None)
      else None,
    )
    if prompted is None:
      console.print("[yellow]Geannuleerd — niets opgeslagen.[/yellow]")
      return 2
    p_date, p_description, p_category, p_amount, _p_checking = prompted
    # Date-based dispatch: future → expected register, today/past → actual.
    if p_date > date.today().isoformat():
      console.print("[dim]→ expected-register (financials expect).[/dim]")
      return add_expected(
        iso_date=p_date,
        description=p_description,
        category=p_category,
        amount=p_amount,
        dry_run=dry_run,
      )
    iso_date, description, category, amount = p_date, p_description, p_category, p_amount

  error = _validate(iso_date, description, category, amount or 0.0, ledger)
  if error:
    console.print(f"[red]Niet opgeslagen: {error}[/red]")
    return 2

  if dry_run:
    projected, _parent = projected_checking(ledger, iso_date, amount or 0.0)
    console.print("[yellow]Dry-run — niets opgeslagen. Zou toevoegen:[/yellow]")
    console.print(
      f"  {iso_date}  {description}  [{category}]  {amount:+,.2f} → checking {projected:,.2f}"
    )
    return 0

  mutation, entry = cmd_add(
    iso_date=iso_date,
    description=description.strip(),
    category=category,
    amount=amount or 0.0,
    journal=journal,
  )
  if entry is None:
    console.print("[red]Niet opgeslagen: onverwacht leeg resultaat.[/red]")
    return 2
  balances = entry.balances
  console.print(f"[green]Opgeslagen als {entry.id}[/green]")
  console.print(
    f"  {entry.date.isoformat()}  {entry.description}  [{entry.category}]  "
    f"{(entry.postings.get('checking') or 0.0):+,.2f} → checking "
    f"{balances.get('checking', 0.0):,.2f}, spaar {balances.get('savings', 0.0):,.2f}"
    f"  (status: actual)"
  )
  return 0

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The recurring-entry machinery whose projected instances the bookkeeper can suppress one occurrence of.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The recurrence engine projects recurring-payment rules onto future dates as virtual rows (instances) in the ledger view. When the bookkeeper removes an instance id, the engine records that occurrence as an exception of the rule itself: the instance disappears from the projection while the rule keeps running for the remaining periods. It reloads its store fresh before saving (the scan-time rule object never persists), and refuses a second suppression of the same occurrence. Its interest in this process: keeping projected and actual books distinguishable — suppression is a planning act, never a ledger mutation.

# src/financials/recurrence_cli.py — lines 816–848
def suppress_occurrence(entry_id: str) -> int:
  """The delete-wired suppression: 'delete <r-id>' lands here. The
  occurrence's date joins the rule's exceptions (idempotent), so the
  instance disappears from the projection while the rule keeps running
  for the remaining periods. Returns 2 when the id is not a rule
  instance (delete's other resolvers own those)."""
  hit = _find_instance(entry_id)
  if hit is None:
    return 2  # not a projected instance id
  rule_hit, occurrence_date = hit
  console.print(
    f"Instantie van regel: {rule_hit.description} — {rule_hit.amount:+,.2f} "
    f"[{rule_hit.category}] op {occurrence_date.isoformat()}"
  )
  if occurrence_date.isoformat() in rule_hit.exceptions:
    console.print("[yellow]Deze instantie is al onderdrukt.[/yellow]")
    return 0
  answer = Prompt.ask("Type 'ja' om te bevestigen", default="")
  if answer.strip().lower() != "ja":
    console.print("[dim]Geannuleerd — niets gewijzigd.[/dim]")
    return 2
  # Re-load fresh (same content-match discipline as edit_occurrence's
  # exception path): rule_hit belongs to the scan's list.
  rules = load_recurrences()
  for rule in rules:
    if rule.description == rule_hit.description and rule.category == rule_hit.category:
      rule.exceptions = sorted(set(rule.exceptions) | {occurrence_date.isoformat()})
  save_recurrences(rules)
  console.print(
    f"[green]Instantie onderdrukt ({occurrence_date.isoformat()}); de regel "
    "blijft de overige periodes draaien.[/green]"
  )
  return 0

A committed correction rebooks the row by removing and re-inserting it
Title
docs.text: A committed correction rebooks the row by removing and re-inserting it

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Applying a field correction to the ledger takes the row out at its current position and re-inserts the corrected full row, so running balances re-derive from both steps.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The ledger's update is a delete-then-insert of the same row identity; corrections recompute the running totals around the changed row.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A field correction changes date, description, category or amount — any of which can shift the row's position in the date-ordered ledger or the amounts it posts. The ledger implements the correction as two balance-correct primitives on the same row identity: the existing row is removed (its postings reversed against every later row) and the corrected row is inserted at its new date position (its postings applied to every later row). The row keeps its identity — references held elsewhere by related entries stay valid — and every later row's running totals are recomputed exactly once per direction. The result: the corrected row lands in the right order with the right values, and the checkbook totals of all later rows re-derive correctly.

def cmd_update(
  target: str,
  iso_date: str,
  description: str,
  category: str,
  amount: float,
  journal: Journal | None = None,
) -> tuple[Mutation, Transaction | None]:
  """Append an update (full replacement of the mutable fields; the id
  and linked references ride along; date moves re-insert) and apply it.
  Returns (mutation, applied entry); entry is None for an unknown
  target — callers guard that beforehand."""
  mutation = UpdateMutation(
    target=target,
    date=Date(iso_date),
    description=description,
    category=category,
    postings=postings_for(category, amount),
  )
  ledger = append_and_apply(mutation, journal)
  entry, _ = ledger.find(target)
  return mutation, entry

def _resolve_ledger_target(fix_id: str, ledger: Ledger) -> LedgerTransaction | None:
  """Resolve a fix's target in the committed ledger: full hash id or
  unambiguous prefix. Raises on ambiguity; None when absent."""
  if not fix_id:
    raise ValueError("fix has no id")
  matches = [t for t in ledger.transactions if t.id and (t.id == fix_id or t.id.startswith(fix_id))]
  if len(matches) > 1:
    raise ValueError(f"ambiguous id prefix in fix: {fix_id} ({len(matches)} matches)")
  return matches[0] if matches else None

def find_entry(
  entry_id: str, transactions: list[Transaction], expected: list[Transaction]
) -> Transaction | None:
  """Resolve an id within the provided stores — prefix-scoped: t####
  searches the actual register only, e#### the expected register only
  (the documented id contract; regression: an e-id colliding with an
  actual row used to resolve to the actual row while remove_row routed
  by prefix, deleting the other store's row). Committed rows resolve in
  the LEDGER (ledger.find); this helper is for the expected register and
  callers holding explicit lists. None when absent."""
  if entry_id.startswith("e") and entry_id[1:].isdigit():
    for t in expected:
      if t.id == entry_id:
        return t
    return None
  for t in transactions:
    if t.id == entry_id:
      return t
  return None

The toggle is idempotent: pausing an already-paused rule (or resuming an active one) reports the state and changes nothing.

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: When the rule's due date arrives, a committed transaction with the same category and the same amount (within a cent) dated within five days of the due date stands in for the projected instance, which the forecast then drops.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Superseding — the forecast shows the rule instance until actual money with matching category, amount and timing covers it; then the projection yields to the real row.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The forecast never double-counts a bill that was actually paid. For each projected instance the planner looks at the committed history around the due date: if a real transaction in the same category carries the same amount (to within a cent) and sits within five days either side of the due date in the same year, the projection skips the instance and the real booking stands alone in the view. This is what makes the rules a forecast layer rather than a duplicate ledger: the moment real money shows up, the planned row retires for that period without anyone closing it. Rules whose pattern drifts (a real payment at a different amount) are handled by the approval process's exception recording, not by this matching.

def _covers(occurrence: date, rule: Recurrence, transactions: list[Transaction]) -> bool:
  """True when a real transaction covers this rule instance's period."""
  window_lo = occurrence - timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  window_hi = occurrence + timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  for t in transactions:
    if not t.date or not t.date.startswith(str(occurrence.year)):

    t_date = date.fromisoformat(t.date)
    if not (window_lo <= t_date <= window_hi):

    if t.category != rule.category:

    if t.amount_eur is None or abs(t.amount_eur - rule.amount) > AMOUNT_TOLERANCE:

    return True

def cmd_delete(target: str, journal: Journal | None = None) -> tuple[Mutation, bool]:
  """Append a delete carrying the victim's full pre-image (read from
  the live ledger BEFORE the append) and apply it. Returns (mutation,
  deleted) — False when the target is unknown (nothing appended)."""
  journal = journal or command_journal()
  ledger = load_ledger(journal)
  victim, _ = ledger.find(target)
  if victim is None:
    return DeleteMutation(  # nothing appended: nothing happened
      date=Date("1970-01-01"),
      description="",
      category="",
      postings={},
      target=target,
    ), False
  mutation = DeleteMutation(
    date=victim.date,
    description=victim.description,
    category=victim.category,
    postings=dict(victim.postings),
    linked=list(victim.linked),
    target=target,
  )
  append_and_apply(mutation, journal)
  return mutation, True

docs.text: When a planned entry that has already landed (dated today or earlier) is edited with every field accepted as-is, the all-Enter session counts as intent to confirm — the plan is booked into the ledger with its planned values.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Editing a landed plan is expected to confirm it — accepting all current values with only Enters books the plan as-is.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A planned entry dated today or in the past has "landed" — the plan is due. The natural business case: the editor notices the landed state and the empty form results and treats the all-Enter pass as confirm intent, booking the plan into the ledger with the planned values, without re-asking anything. Only when there is something to change does the edit form's ordinary path apply — and even then, if the edited date is today or earlier, the edited values confirm into the ledger rather than staying as a plan.

def _confirm_to_actual(t: Transaction, changes: dict) -> int:
  """Edit-to-today-or-past on an expected row: append a ConfirmMutation
  (the e-row retires and the actual lands in one mutation) and drop the
  expected row — only after the confirm applied."""

  description = changes.get("description", t.description)
  category = changes.get("category", t.category)
  amount = changes.get("amount_eur", t.amount_eur)
  if amount is None:
    console.print("[red]Niet omgezet: deze rij heeft geen bedrag.[/red]")
    return 2

  journal = command_journal()

    iso_date=iso_date,
    description=description,
    category=category,
    amount=amount,
    retires=[t.id],
    journal=journal,

  if entry is None:
    console.print("[red]Niet omgezet: geen voorgaande rij gevonden.[/red]")
    return 2

  expected = load_expected()
  save_expected([x for x in expected if x.id != t.id])
  balances = entry.balances
  console.print(
    f"[green]Bevestigd: {t.id} → {entry.id}[/green]  [dim]expected entry verwijderd[/dim]"

An instance whose commit drifts is recorded as an exception
Title
docs.text: An instance whose commit drifts is recorded as an exception

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: When an instance's confirming booking does not still count as covering the rule's period — the amount drifted beyond tolerance or the date moved outside the window — the occurrence is recorded as an exception on the rule so the unconfirmed instance no longer lingers in the open view.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A confirm that changed the values commits the real booking and additionally records the occurrence date as a rule exception, so the stale projection leaves the backlog.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The recurring-projection supersedes an instance only when a real booking still matches the rule's period — same category, amount within a cent of tolerance, date within the few-day window around the rule day. When the confirming booking strays outside that envelope (the bookkeeper interactively adjusted the date or amount), it still commits as the real money, but the projection machinery would keep showing the original instance as due forever. So the confirmation also records the occurrence date among the rule's exception dates — the rule's own list of dates exempt from expansion — closing the loop: the real booking stands, the projected ghost leaves.

# src/financials/recurrences.py — lines 110–125
def _covers(occurrence: date, rule: Recurrence, transactions: list[Transaction]) -> bool:
  """True when a real transaction covers this rule instance's period."""
  window_lo = occurrence - timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  window_hi = occurrence + timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  for t in transactions:
    if not t.date or not t.date.startswith(str(occurrence.year)):
      continue
    t_date = date.fromisoformat(t.date)
    if not (window_lo <= t_date <= window_hi):
      continue
    if t.category != rule.category:
      continue
    if t.amount_eur is None or abs(t.amount_eur - rule.amount) > AMOUNT_TOLERANCE:
      continue
    return True
  return False

DAY_WINDOW = 5  # days around the rule day that a covering transaction may sit
RULE_LOOKBACK_DAYS = 35  # the view's grace lookback before the ledger's anchor

Title
docs.text: Confirming a plan books today through the same doors as any booking

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: The booking created by confirmation carries the plan's values, posts to checking (mirrored into savings for a transfer), and retires the plan identifier in the same mutation; it is chained from the current ledger tip like any manually recorded booking.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A confirmation is a normal booking on the books — same balance bookkeeping, same transfer mirror, same content-hash identity — plus the plan it retires recorded on the committed row.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A confirmed payment is not special money: it flows through the same booking path the bookkeeper uses when recording anything by hand. The bank balances move the same way — checking carries the amount, and a transfer also moves the savings mirror — and the new row joins the ledger at its date position like any other recording, with running balances propagated and its own content-derived identity. What distinguishes it is one line of business content: the committed row carries the retired plan's identifier alongside itself, so the books show which plan this payment settled. The next planned payment in the register then balances off this row exactly as it would have off the tip.

@dataclass
class ConfirmMutation(AddMutation):
  op: str = field(default="confirm", init=False)

  def apply_on(self, ledger: "Ledger") -> Transaction | None:
    existing, _ = ledger.find(self.id or "")
    if existing:  # idempotent re-apply
      return existing
    return ledger.insert(
      Transaction(
        id=self.id,
        date=self.date,
        description=self.description,
        category=self.category,
        postings=self.postings,
        linked=[*self.retires, *self.linked],
      )
    )

# src/financials/commands.py — lines 88–95
def postings_for(category: str, amount: float) -> dict[str, float]:
  """The posting set for an amount in a category: checking carries the
  amount; a transfer carries the savings mirror (the engine moves both
  balances)."""
  postings = {"checking": round(amount, 2)}
  if category == "Overdracht":
    postings["savings"] = round(-amount, 2)
  return postings

Rule Statement
docs.text: Confirming a plan whose payment already sits in the books — a committed identifier, or an instance already covered by a matching booked amount — is a no-op that changes no store.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Confirmation is idempotent — the already-real entry is recognized and reported as nothing-to-do, and no duplicate booking is created.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The books must never grow a second copy of the same payment. Confirming an identifier that already points at a committed booking returns with a note that the row is already actual and nothing was done. The same recognition works at the projection level for rule instances: when a real booking covering the instance's period is already on the books — matching category, amount within tolerance, and date inside the window around the rule day — the instance is skipped as already covered instead of committing a second booking. The open view thus drains without risk of double payment.

Title
docs.text: Confirming an entry removes it from the expected register

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: After a confirming booking applies successfully, the confirmed expected entry is struck from the expected register so it disappears from the open backlog.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The confirmation is not done until the plan is gone — the register row is dropped only after the booking has applied, never before.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The one-step confirmation makes the plan disappear by making it real: once the confirming booking has actually applied to the books, the plan row is struck from the expected register. The order matters and is deliberate — the register is only touched after the booking succeeded, so a failed booking never deletes a plan and the bookkeeper can simply retry. No record of the plan itself is kept in the actual books beyond the booking that retired it; the register simply shrinks. Confirmation therefore is the plan's only exit into recorded money.

Title
docs.text: Detected values are proposals until the bookkeeper approves each field

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: An approved proposal reaches the rule store only through the seeded review loop — every detected value is shown, Enter keeps it, typing replaces it, quitting aborts — and validation failing after the loop still stores nothing.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The approval gate — detection fills the editor's answers, nothing saves until the bookkeeper walks every field and the rule clears validation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Adopting a detected pattern is not a one-keystroke accept: the bookkeeper meets every detected value as the default answer of a question (description, category, amount, cadence, day or weekday anchor, start and optional end date), keeps it with Enter or overwrites it by typing. Nothing reaches the rule store until the loop finishes; a quit mid-way leaves the store untouched with an explicit nothing-saved message. The same conversation shape serves hand-added rules (missing fields asked, defaults offered), editing a rule, and editing a single occurrence — one approval grammar for every change to the rule book. Fully-flagged hand-add invocations skip the questions entirely; their flags are the bookkeeper's answers.

docs.title: Every mutation is content hash identified and journal verified
Every mutation is content-hash identified and journal-verified
Title
docs.text: Every mutation is content-hash identified and journal-verified

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Each business change is recorded as a mutation whose identity is a content hash of its canonical form plus a creation timestamp; it is appended to an append-only journal, and the ledger rebuilt from it verifies hash and timestamps on read.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Intake writes are append-only journal mutations hashed over canonical content + creation time, replayable and verifiable — two identical recordings still get distinct identities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The books' integrity model: nothing is edited in place. A recording (add, confirm, update, delete) becomes one mutation object, stamped with a creation timestamp and identified by a content hash over its canonical fields. The mutation is appended to the journal file; the ledger is rebuilt by folding checkpoint plus tail replay, and each applied row carries a row hash guarding its content and balances, re-verified when the ledger is read. The timestamp guarantees two byte-identical recordings on the same day still get genuinely distinct identities, so neither history nor hash-collisions can conflate them. Openings are not special: the first posting to an account creates it.

"""Journal (append-only mutations) + ledger (applied transactions).

Identity vs integrity (decided 2026-09-18, docs/journaled-ledger.md):
  - a MUTATION's id IS its anti-corruption validator: 16-hex content
    hash over the canonical mutation minus the id (rehash on read)
  - a TRANSACTION's id is assigned ONCE by its creating mutation
    (add | confirm) and never recomputed — updates and balance
    propagation keep it, so linked/retires never need scanning
  - a transaction carries a separate stored `hash` (content hash minus
    the hash field, balances included) guarding its row on disk;
    recomputed by every writer (insert, update, propagate)
  - identical mutation content needs distinct ids (two Q8 rows): every
    mutation carries `ts` (creation time, hashed content) so content
    hashes never collide between two real entries
Ops: add | update | delete | confirm — no opening op (openings are
ordinary add transactions; the first posting to an account creates it).

def append_and_apply(mutation: Mutation, journal: Journal | None = None) -> Ledger:
  """THE single write step: stamp ts, append the mutation, boot the
  ledger (checkpoint + tail replay — the just-appended mutation rides
  the tail), and persist the converged checkpoint. Returns the live
  ledger for feedback (find the applied entry by mutation id)."""
  journal = journal or command_journal()
  if not mutation.ts:
    mutation.ts = next(_clock)
  if not mutation.id:
    mutation.id = mutation.content_hash
  journal.append(mutation)
  ledger = load_ledger(journal)
  checkpoint(journal)
  return ledger

  def rehash(self) -> None:
    """Recompute the row's on-disk guard: content hash minus the hash
    field (includes the id, so id swaps are caught too)."""
    payload = {key: value for key, value in self.asdict().items() if key != "hash"}
    self.hash = hashlib.sha256(canonical(payload).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]

  def verify(self) -> bool:
    payload = {key: value for key, value in self.asdict().items() if key != "hash"}
    expected = hashlib.sha256(canonical(payload).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]
    return self.hash == expected

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A new actual entry's opening balance for the projection is taken from the ledger row dated immediately before the entry's date — the same row the engine will chain from — so an inserted backdated entry re-chains balances around it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Balance chaining positions a new entry by its date, taking the predecessor row the engine will chain from — so past-dated inserts re-thread the running balances rather than only appending.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Where a row lands in the running books depends on its date, not on when it is recorded. So a forgotten spend recorded days later lands at its true date: rows after it are re-chained, and the running balances stay meaningful. Without a predecessor row at all (the ledger has nothing before this date yet) the recording is refused — the engine cannot state balances it has no base for.

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A varying-amount pattern is proposed only when every occurrence pushes the same direction — all incomes or all spends; occurrences of both signs never form one pattern.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Tier B's uniform-sign guardrail — a group with both positive and negative amounts is turned away rather than proposed as one rule.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When the amounts in a repeating group vary (the budget-style case: the same bill paid at different sizes each period), the detector still proposes the pattern — but only when the group moves money in one direction consistently. A description that sometimes earns and sometimes spends is not one repeating payment, and the code turns it away rather than inventing a rule with a median that describes neither case. Constant-amount patterns are exempt from this check only in the sense that near-identical amounts are effectively same-signed anyway; the guardrail is stated for the varying case. The proposal therefore never smuggles opposite flows of money into one scheduled entry.

docs.title: The detector proposes only regularly spaced patterns with enough occurrences
The detector proposes only regularly spaced patterns with enough occurrences
Title
docs.text: The detector proposes only regularly spaced patterns with enough occurrences

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A pattern group earns a proposal only when its occurrences share description and category, sit on a regular weekly, biweekly, monthly or yearly spacing, and appear at least min_occurrences times in the committed history.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The detector's candidacy bar — same description and category, a spacing band that classifies, and at least three (configurable) actual occurrences.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When the bookkeeper asks the tool to spot repeating payments, it groups the committed history's actual rows by description and category and only speaks up when a group is a genuine pattern. Rows without a date, without an amount or with a zero amount are ignored from the start. A group must hold at least the minimum number of occurrences (three by default) and the gaps between the occurrence dates must fall inside one of four regularity bands — roughly weekly (5–9 days), every other week (11–17 days), monthly (26–38 days) or yearly (360–372 days). Two proposal shapes exist: near-identical amounts (within about five percent of the median) propose that median, and timely-but-varying amounts propose the median too but with the observed range shown honestly. A pattern that misses all bands or the count bar produces no proposal at all — silence, not a guessed rule.

def _classify_frequency(dates: list[date], min_occurrences: int) -> str | None:
  """Classify sorted dates by their gap bands (weekly 5-9, biweekly 11-17,
  monthly 26-38, yearly 360-372); None when no band holds enough gaps.
  Non-overlapping bands, checked most-specific first — a skipped week
  (gap ≈ 14) inside a weekly streak still classifies weekly."""
  gaps = [(b - a).days for a, b in zip(dates, dates[1:], strict=False)]
  for frequency, lo, hi in (
    ("weekly", 5, 9),
    ("biweekly", 11, 17),
    ("monthly", 26, 38),
    ("yearly", 360, 372),
  ):
    if len([g for g in gaps if lo <= g <= hi]) >= min_occurrences - 1:
      return frequency
  return None

docs.text: An all-Enter edit session changes nothing; exactly the re-typed fields become the correction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The prompted edit is deliberately a whole-form pass: the bookkeeper walks all four fields (date, description, category, amount) with each pre-filled at the current value. Keeping a value is one Enter. Anything untouched produces no change. Two consequences in business terms — walking the whole form and accepting everything leaves the entry exactly as it was (for a planned entry that case is treated as confirmation intent, separately); and the eventual correction carries only what truly changed. The form is also the guard: a description must be non-empty, dates must parse, amounts must parse as signed numbers; three failed attempts at any field abandon the whole session.

def _collect_changes(t: Transaction, actual: bool) -> dict | None:
  """Prompt all four fields pre-filled; return only the changed fields
  (keyed by Transaction field name). None = user aborted."""

  iso_date = ""
  for _ in range(RETRY_LIMIT):
    text = Prompt.ask("Datum (YYYY-MM-DD)", default=t.date).strip()

  if not description:

    return None

  category = ask_category(current=t.category)
  if category == ABORT or category is None:

    return None
  amount = _ask_amount(t.amount_eur, allow_zero=not actual)
  if amount is None:

  changes: dict = {}

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: When applying all pending change-sets, the files are processed in name order, oldest first, each fully applied and renamed before the next begins.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Pending files sort by name and apply one at a time; a failed file stops the sweep before it is renamed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The sweep collects every pending cleanup file in the data directory that carries a recognized format extension, sorts them so the oldest name comes first, and applies them one at a time. Each file completes fully — every fix in it applied and journaled — before it is renamed and the sweep moves on. Because an exception aborts the file before its rename, a failure leaves that file pending and halts the sweep: the bookkeeper resolves the file (editing it or removing it) and reruns; the successfully applied files before it stay applied. When nothing is pending the sweep simply reports that.

def postings_for(category: str, amount: float) -> dict[str, float]:
  """The posting set for an amount in a category: checking carries the

docs.title: components
docs.text:
A structural unit of the analyzed system: one cohesive area of related functionality, named by its role, implemented within a bounded, nameable set of modules, and exposed to its consumers — other code or actors — through the interface it presents.

Fact Sheet Name cleanup fix engine confirmation dispatcher expected register store interactive deletion dispatcher interactive entry editor journaled ledger engine recurrence engine transaction entry interface

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The engine that takes reviewed change-set files of row corrections and applies them one fix at a time to the live journaled ledger, refusing anything it cannot resolve.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A structural unit: the reader, resolver and applier for reviewed cleanup change-sets. It loads a file of fixes (its preferred format reads one named section of tables, with a JSON fallback), splits the fixes into field corrections and whole-row operations, and applies each kind through its dedicated path: field corrections rebook one ledger row each, whole-row operations remove committed rows or clear parked plans from the expected register. It owns the resolution discipline — each fix must name one row, known and unambiguous — and the from-guard that refuses a correction whose stated old value no longer matches. It also owns the pending sweep that applies every unconsumed change-set file oldest first and renames each one when done. Other modules resolve the canonical journal location through this unit. Consumers: the fix command surface drives it from its two modes; the removal and reporting flows borrow its whole-row path and its journal-location view.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The dispatcher that routes a landed plan, rule instance or group of either to its matching one-step commit path.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A structural unit: the one-step route that turns a landed but planned entry into recorded money. It presents a single confirm command that accepts any open entry id — a plan row, a recurring-rule instance, or a group of them — decides which store the id belongs to, and routes each shape to its own commit path. For plans it runs the confirm-and-retire commit; for rule instances the rule's own values commit with no further questions; for groups it walks the members in date order and keeps the group intact. It also owns the picker view the bookkeeper meets when confirming with no id in mind, and the safety notes that flag a future-dated plan refused before anything changes. Consumers: the CLI dispatcher imports it for the confirm command, and tests exercise it end to end. Its boundary to the entry interface is clean — that unit records new money interactively; this unit commits already-known values without a conversation.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The interactive removal surface behind the financials delete command — resolves the id, prints the row, and routes to the matching removal path.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A structural unit: the dialog the bookkeeper meets for taking an entry off the books. It exposes the deletion command surface, decides what a typed id means by consulting each store in order — committed ledger rows, planned entries, groupings, projected rule instances — and routes each shape to its own removal path. It owns the bare-delete picker menu, the row display, the explicit confirmation prompt (typed yes required; Enter cancels), the success and refusal feedback, and the transfer-specific warning. Consumers: the CLI dispatcher binds the delete command to it, and the delete-focused tests exercise every store path end to end. Its boundary is clean — this unit decides and routes; the journaled engine applies actual deletions, the expected store loses its row directly, and rule instances and groups speak to their own machinery.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The interactive editor behind the financials edit command — resolves the entry, prompts the corrected fields pre-filled, and routes the correction to the ledger or the planned-entry register.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The entry editor is the interactive correction surface of the household bookkeeping app. It resolves the target entry from the given id — a committed ledger row (full id or prefix), a planned entry, a group, or a recurring-entry instance — and, given no id at all, lets the bookkeeper pick from the last ten actual rows. It shows the current row, then walks one prompted form for date, description, category, and amount, each pre-filled with the current value; only fields the bookkeeper actually changed are applied. It owns the branching that decides where a correction lands — a committed row edited to a future date moves to the planned-entry register, a committed row edited to today or earlier is journaled as a full replacement, a planned entry edited toward today or the past is confirmed into the ledger, and a planned entry edited further ahead is rewritten in the register. Every journaled route goes through the journal-native command mutations, so a correction is provable later in the journal rather than a silent overwrite of history.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The mutation-journal machinery that turns each recording into a content-hashed, replayable mutation applied to the running ledger.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A structural unit: the append-only mutation journal and the ledger it folds into. Every business change to the books is one mutation object (add, confirm, update, delete) carrying the business fields + postings; the engine stamps a creation time, assigns the mutation's identity as a content hash of its canonical form, appends it to the journal file, replays the journal onto the ledger, and persists the converged checkpoint. The ledger applies a mutation by inserting the transaction at its date position, computing the category postings and propagating running balances forward to every later row. Every transaction row carries a row hash guarding its content and balances, verified when the ledger is read back. Consumers: the entry interface, corrections surfaces and reporting all read or fold this engine; the bookkeeper experiences it as "the entry is saved and the balance is right".

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The household books' two-sided world — movements that happened (journaled, balance-carrying) versus movements planned (parked, balance-free).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The product's central distinction. An entry is either actual — it happened on a past or present day, lives in the journaled ledger, and carries the running balances it produced — or expected — it is planned for a future day, lives in its own register, and carries no balances. The date of a recorded movement decides its side, and the confirm path is the only bridge between them. The intake surface polices the boundary in both directions: future-dated input is diverted to the register, and a recording claiming a past day while a future row outranks it is warned about and refused.

Pre-image (the victim's content at removal time)
Summary
docs.text: The pre-image is the removed entry's complete content at the moment of removal, carried inside the removal record so history can rebuild and prove what was deleted.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When an actual transaction is removed, the code speaks of the victim's pre-image — a snapshot of the entry exactly as it stood: date, description, category, its account postings, its links to other rows. docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A rule instance is a virtual row that a recurring-payment rule projects onto a future date — real in the forecast, never in the books.

docs.text: The recurrence engine projects each rule onto dates as instances, shown in the ledger view with their own ids. An instance is not a transaction — no money moved and nothing is committed. docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The detector's second tier — timely patterns whose amounts differ period to period are proposed at their median with the observed range shown.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The household's budget-style pattern: the same recurring bill is confirmed every period with the actual spend, which varies. The detector's first tier (near-identical amounts) would reject these; the second tier recognizes them. When a group's dates classify as a regular cadence but its amounts do not agree within the near-identical band, the detector proposes the median amount as the rule's nominal value and attaches the observed low-to-high range so the bookkeeper reviews the spread honestly. The design deliberately allows a wide spread: proposals cost only a glance because nothing saves without approval, so no magnitude cap is imposed. The uniform-sign guardrail stands — a group that moves money both ways is not one pattern.

docs.title: Weekday anchor weekly and biweekly phase
Summary
docs.text: For weekly and biweekly rules, the start date itself is the schedule's phase — the anchor every future instance is spaced from.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Weekly and biweekly rules schedule by phase, not by day-of-month: their start date is the first occurrence, and every following instance sits an exact multiple of seven or fourteen days from it. The bookkeeper can give a weekday word (the Dutch single letters or their English forms) instead of a date — typing one snaps the start date forward to that weekday, so the anchor is what makes the rule land on the intended day. The design note in the code explains why the anchor must be stored rather than derived: instance identities are derived from the rule's content, so the schedule must be reconstructible from the rule alone, deterministically, forever.

# src/financials/recurrences.py — lines 90–106
  elif rule.frequency in ("weekly", "biweekly"):
    # Weekly/biweekly anchor on the rule's start date (the phase): the
    # first instance IS start (when inside the window), then every k*7
    # days. Deterministic — instance ids are content hashes, so the
    # schedule must be reconstructible from the rule alone.
    if not rule.start:
      return dates  # phase anchor missing: nothing to expand
    anchor = date.fromisoformat(rule.start)
    step = 7 if rule.frequency == "weekly" else 14
    # first anchor multiple >= start
    k = 0
    instance = anchor + timedelta(days=k * step)
    while instance <= end:
      if instance >= start:
        dates.append(instance)
      k += 1
      instance = anchor + timedelta(days=k * step)

# src/financials/recurrence_cli.py — lines 121–138
def _snap_to_weekday(anchor: str, weekday_text: str) -> str | None:
  """Snap an ISO anchor date forward to the given weekday (today when the
  anchor is empty). A bare weekday name returns the next such weekday on
  or after the anchor; an ISO date passes through unchanged (its own
  weekday IS the anchor). None when unparseable."""
  base = anchor or TODAY().isoformat()
  try:
    base_date = date.fromisoformat(base)
  except ValueError:
    return None
  needle = (weekday_text or "").strip().lower()
  if not needle:
    return base  # keep the anchor's own weekday
  offset = _WEEKDAY_ALIASES.get(needle)
  if offset is None:
    return None  # not a weekday alias: caller keeps the base anchor
  delta = (offset - base_date.weekday()) % 7
  return (base_date + timedelta(days=delta)).isoformat()

docs.title: Single write route through append and apply
Convention Statement
docs.text: Every store-writing command funnels its mutation through one helper that stamps the timestamp, sets the content-hash id, appends to the journal, folds the ledger and persists the checkpoint.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Repo convention: commands never write stores directly — one shared write path owns stamping, id assignment, append, fold and checkpoint persist.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The mutations surface (add / edit / delete / confirm) is built so every command builds a mutation object and hands it to the same append-and-apply helper; the journal docstring records this as the decided design ("Journal-native command mutations"). No intake path writes a ledger or register file by hand. The convention keeps the integrity model enforceable in one place and makes the write path auditable by reading one function.

# src/financials/commands.py — lines 1–14
"""Journal-native command mutations (roadmap step 6): every mutating
command (add / edit / delete / fixes) builds a mutation, appends it to
the canonical journal, and persists the checkpoint. There is no
intermediate store: the journal IS the store of record, the ledger's
engine owns balance chaining and date ordering, and ledger.json is the
snapshot the next boot hydrates from.

Mutation ids are content hashes (one hash scheme end-to-end); machine
paths stamp a monotonic ts so identical content still yields distinct
ids (the Q8 lesson). Command failures happen BEFORE the append: a
rejected command leaves no journal line, so every line records a
change that actually happened.
"""

# src/financials/commands.py — lines 72–85
def append_and_apply(mutation: Mutation, journal: Journal | None = None) -> Ledger:
  """THE single write step: stamp ts, append the mutation, boot the
  ledger (checkpoint + tail replay — the just-appended mutation rides
  the tail), and persist the converged checkpoint. Returns the live
  ledger for feedback (find the applied entry by mutation id)."""
  journal = journal or command_journal()
  if not mutation.ts:
    mutation.ts = next(_clock)
  if not mutation.id:
    mutation.id = mutation.content_hash
  journal.append(mutation)
  ledger = load_ledger(journal)
  checkpoint(journal)
  return ledger

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A parked future plan — a dated, categorised, pre-recorded movement that stays fixed and unapplied until it is confirmed against the actual books.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: One movement parked in the expected register: the same cashflow shape as an actual row, stored with the status that marks it as a plan. It is written once at intake and never modified — only re-read or removed. No balance is projected for it: nothing has happened yet, so it carries no running-balance position until the day it is confirmed against the journaled ledger. Its id is assigned sequentially within the register store, not by content hash — identity rests on the register's fixed rows, not their content.

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: Two statuses with a hard wall between them: "expected" — created once by the register's add path, stored in the register's own file, read and removed — and "actual", which an expected entry never takes in place; the register holds plans, and the actual books materialise them only via a confirm recording that retires the plan's id. Balance fields stay empty for the whole parked life. The add surface routes future-dated input here, and the intake-time validation guarantees nothing dated today or earlier can be parked.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The applied running-balance row in the actual books — one dated movement with its postings, resulting balances and integrity hash.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The stored unit of the actual books. Each row is the applied form of one journal mutation: a dated, described movement in an approved category, the postings it makes against accounts, the running balances it results in, and a row hash guarding its content. Rows also carry the raw-parsed legacy fields from the retired importer (kept so the store shape stays flexible) and a status distinguishing actual rows from rows still parked as expected. A row's identity is assigned once by its creating mutation and never recomputed — updates and balance propagation keep it, so links between rows stay stable.

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: State lives entirely in fields: the balances dict carries the running balance position each row results in, computed by the engine at apply-time (insert positions the row by date, then propagates balances forward through every later row); the hash field is recomputed by every writer (insert, update, propagate) and verified when the ledger is read back; status is fixed by the path of record (actual for journaled rows, expected for parked plans); linked_id connects a settled plan to the row that settled it. The row's id is assigned once by its creating mutation — identity never derived from content.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: One standing recurring payment rule — the pattern from which planned instances are projected and to which confirmations report back.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A recurring bill or income held as a rule rather than as stored rows. From the rule's pattern the views project a planned instance for each due date; confirmation books the rule's own values for the instance and, when the committing booking no longer matches the rule's period, records that specific occurrence as an exception so it stops appearing as due. The rule therefore both supplies the confirmation's values and receives its aftermath. Rules can be paused by deactivation; inactive rules project nothing and their instances can no longer be confirmed.

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: The rule file is the only place recurrence state lives; instances are never stored — they are recomputed by expansion from description/category/amount/frequency/day/month and the start/end bounds. Two bits of mutable state ride inside the rule: the active flag (an inactive rule stops projecting and can no longer be confirmed) and the exceptions list (ISO occurrence dates exempt from expansion — grown by a drifted confirmation commit, which is how a confirmed-but-changed instance is retired from the projection). Confirmation never edits the pattern fields; it only writes exceptions.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The parsed quick-add parts — date, amount, category and description — where any part may be missing, and a missing part is asked for, never assumed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The intermediate record of the quick-add line: whatever the bookkeeper's one-line input actually contained, split into date, amount, category and description. It is a pre-fill, not a transaction: it only seeds the prompts for whichever parts are present, and everything the line omitted is asked for. The parser treats a token that looks like an amount (sign or currency marker) as intentional — an unparseable such token is an outright error rather than description text swallowed by accident.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A named bundle of open rows — plans and rule instances together — that confirms member by member while the group itself keeps standing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A bookkeeper-made bundle that groups related money moments — a holiday's costs, a bill's installments — under one label, date and category for the views. Its members are identifiers of rows in the other stores or projections, not copies: a member may be a parked plan, a booked row, or a rule instance. That is why confirmation moves through it unchanged: the group lists who belongs, and when a member's identifier changes during confirming, the group's membership list is re-pointed so it keeps showing the same real-world rows. The rollup row a group projects is display-only; confirming the group never stores one.

docs.title: Group confirm exit codes report partial success as full success
Group confirm exit codes report partial success as full success
Title
docs.text: Group confirm exit codes report partial success as full success

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Should the confirm command report a partially-confirmed group as success (today's behavior — exit 0 with skip notes), or should the skipped members surface as a distinct failure-like signal so pipelines and scripts can react?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A group confirm that confirms some members and skips others exits 0; only a group with nothing landable exits nonzero — the code's choice, not the business's, is unrecorded anywhere.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When a group is confirmed, future-dated, amountless, unresolvable and already-covered members are each skipped with a on-screen note, while landable members commit; the command then exits as a success. Only the case where nothing at all could be confirmed exits nonzero. # src/financials/recurrences.py — lines 261–275
def _classify_frequency(dates: list[date], min_occurrences: int) -> str | None:
  """Classify sorted dates by their gap bands (weekly 5-9, biweekly 11-17,
  monthly 26-38, yearly 360-372); None when no band holds enough gaps.
  Non-overlapping bands, checked most-specific first — a skipped week
  (gap ≈ 14) inside a weekly streak still classifies weekly."""
  gaps = [(b - a).days for a, b in zip(dates, dates[1:], strict=False)]
  for frequency, lo, hi in (
    ("weekly", 5, 9),
    ("biweekly", 11, 17),
    ("monthly", 26, 38),
    ("yearly", 360, 372),
  ):
    if len([g for g in gaps if lo <= g <= hi]) >= min_occurrences - 1:
      return frequency
  return None

def _covers(occurrence: date, rule: Recurrence, transactions: list[Transaction]) -> bool:
  """True when a real transaction covers this rule instance's period."""
  window_lo = occurrence - timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  window_hi = occurrence + timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  for t in transactions:
    if not t.date or not t.date.startswith(str(occurrence.year)):
      continue
    t_date = date.fromisoformat(t.date)
    if not (window_lo <= t_date <= window_hi):
      continue
    if t.category != rule.category:
      continue
    if t.amount_eur is None or abs(t.amount_eur - rule.amount) > AMOUNT_TOLERANCE:
      continue
    return True
  return False

def find_group(groups: list[Group], id_or_name: str) -> Group | None:
  """Exact id first, then unique id prefix, then the group NAME
  (case-insensitive exact, then unique case-insensitive prefix) —
  `group add Mastercard e0016` addresses the group by name. Ambiguous
  prefixes (two groups 'Mastercard september'/'Mastercard oktober') match
  nothing: ids stay the canonical address."""
  needle = (id_or_name or "").strip()
  if not needle:
    return None
  exact = next((g for g in groups if g.id == needle), None)
  if exact is not None:
    return exact
  hits = [g for g in groups if g.id.startswith(needle)]
  if len(hits) == 1:
    return hits[0]
  lowered = needle.lower()
  by_label = [g for g in groups if g.label.lower() == lowered]
  if len(by_label) == 1:
    return by_label[0]
  by_prefix = [g for g in groups if g.label.lower().startswith(lowered)]
  return by_prefix[0] if len(by_prefix) == 1 else None

def append_and_apply(mutation: Mutation, journal: Journal | None = None) -> Ledger:
  """THE single write step: stamp ts, append the mutation, boot the
  ledger (checkpoint + tail replay — the just-appended mutation rides
  the tail), and persist the converged checkpoint. Returns the live
  ledger for feedback (find the applied entry by mutation id)."""
  journal = journal or command_journal()
  if not mutation.ts:
    mutation.ts = next(_clock)
  if not mutation.id:
    mutation.id = mutation.content_hash
  journal.append(mutation)
  ledger = load_ledger(journal)
  checkpoint(journal)
  return ledger

docs.text: When the engine applies a removal, it takes the removed row's account postings, negates and rounds each to whole cents, splices the row out of the ledger, and then walks every remaining row at and beyond the removed row's position, subtracting the reversal from each row's running balance and re-hashing each row on the way. The bookkeeper's experience: after removing an old entry, every later row shows as if the entry never existed, and each repaired row keeps its own integrity guard. Nothing about this is business policy — it is the arithmetic that makes a removal leave no balance drift behind.

Boot-fold replay with hash-guarded rows and checkpoint convergence
Title
docs.text: Boot-fold replay with hash-guarded rows and checkpoint convergence

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: How the journal makes every append durable and every replay verifiable — checkpoint plus tail replay, each row hash-verified at boot.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The journal stores removals and everything else in one line-per-record file, each record stamped with a creation time and carrying an id that is the content hash of the record's canonical form. Reading the books back never trusts the file blindly — it hydrates the checkpoint, verifies every journal record's hash before applying it, replays only the records after the checkpoint watermark, and refuses to boot anything on a hash mismatch or a checkpoint tip that never appears in the journal. Rebuilds converge after any crash gap — records written beyond the checkpoint replay, and the next persist writes the converged checkpoint. This guards the removal-history rule and the stale-pre-image refusal; the two live inside this replay machinery.

  """THE single write step: stamp ts, append the mutation, boot the

  the tail), and persist the converged checkpoint. Returns the live
  ledger for feedback (find the applied entry by mutation id)."""

    mutation.ts = next(_clock)

    mutation.id = mutation.content_hash

def load_ledger(journal: Journal | Path | str, path: Path | str | None = None) -> Ledger:
  """Roadmap step 5: boot. Rebuild the in-memory ledger from the
  checkpoint (hydrate, hash-guard-verified) and bring it to the journal
  tip by applying the journal tail beyond the checkpoint's watermark —
  the tail replay, per the design. Converges when a gap is healed:
  a crash left the journal ahead, the replay catches up and the next
  persist writes the converged checkpoint.

  Self-healing when no checkpoint exists: a full fold replaces it (the
  in-memory ledger is disposable — fold(journal) reproduces it exactly).
  Structural damage (the checkpoint tip never appears in the journal —
  truncation or reorder) is NOT the hash's job: refuse loudly, the
  tip + backup path own it. Default checkpoint path: journal.jsonl's
  sibling ledger.json."""
  journal = journal if isinstance(journal, Journal) else Journal(journal)
  checkpoint_path = Path(path) if path else journal.path.with_name("ledger.json")
  ledger = Ledger()
  if not checkpoint_path.exists():
    # No checkpoint: self-heal by full fold (and persist it, so the next
    # boot hydrates instead of folding).
    ledger, tip = fold(journal)
    checkpoint(journal, checkpoint_path)
    return ledger
  persisted = json.loads(checkpoint_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
  ledger.hydrate(persisted.get("entries", []))
  watermark = persisted.get("tip", "")
  if not watermark:
    # Empty checkpoint (empty journal at checkpoint time): the tip
    # appears vacuously; a non-empty journal behind an empty checkpoint
    # means the journal arrived AFTER the crash-gap persist — the whole
    # journal replays (seen stays False, treated as all-tail).
    for mutation in journal:
      if mutation.id and mutation.content_hash != mutation.id:
        raise ValueError(
          f"journal row {mutation.id!r} fails its content hash "
          f"(rehashed {mutation.content_hash}) — refusing to boot a corrupt journal: {mutation}"
        )
      ledger.apply(mutation)
    return ledger
  seen = False
  for mutation in journal:
    if mutation.id and mutation.content_hash != mutation.id:
      raise ValueError(
        f"journal row {mutation.id!r} fails its content hash "
        f"(rehashed {mutation.content_hash}) — refusing to boot a corrupt journal: {mutation}"
      )
    if not seen:
      if mutation.id == watermark:
        seen = True
      continue  # before the watermark: already folded into the checkpoint
    ledger.apply(mutation)  # tail beyond the watermark: replay it
  if not seen:
    raise ValueError(
      f"checkpoint tip {watermark!r} never appears in the journal — "
      "truncated or reordered journal (structure damage is the tip's + "
      "backup's job); refusing to boot"
    )
  return ledger

docs.title: Content hash and timestamp mutation identity
Summary
docs.text: The mutation's id is the hash of its canonical content plus a creation timestamp; the timestamp guarantees two identical recordings never collide.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The implementation of identity: the canonical serialization of the mutation (with its creation timestamp) is hashed to 16 hex characters and assigned as the mutation's id before it is appended; the ledger applies the mutation and the applied row keeps that id from then on. Two byte-identical recordings therefore always land as distinct rows — the timestamp rides the hash and cannot be colliding for two real events. Applied rows carry a separate stored hash guarding row content and balances, recomputed by every writer and verified on read-back.

docs.title: Date positioned insert with forward propagation
Summary
docs.text: The engine places a new row at its date position among existing rows and re-runs the balances of every following row.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: How the engine makes an inserted row cohere with the books already saved. The row is inserted into the ledger positioned by its date; its result balance is derived from the closest earlier row (the predecessor), and every later row's balance is recomputed in sequence from the new row's postings. This is the implementation side of the intake's balance chaining: the predecessor the projection took is the same row the insert takes, so confirmed projection and applied result agree.

  def insert(self, transaction: Transaction) -> Transaction:
    """
    idx      0     1          2        3     4     5
    before   Z   parent       X        Y     Z
    after    Z   parent  transaction   X     Y     Z
    """
    parent, idx = self.find_parent(transaction.date)
    balances = parent.balances if parent else {}
    transaction.balances = self.apply_postings(balances, transaction.postings)
    transaction.rehash()
    self.transactions.insert(idx + 1, transaction)
    self.propagate(transaction.postings, idx + 2)
    return transaction

  def propagate(self, changes: dict[str, float], idx: int) -> None:
    while idx < len(self.transactions):
      row = self.transactions[idx]
      row.balances = self.apply_postings(row.balances, changes)
      row.rehash()
      idx += 1

docs.text: The write step stamps a timestamp, mints the record's content-hash identity, appends it, reloads the ledger from the persisted snapshot carrying the new line on its tail, and persists the converged snapshot.

docs.title: Gap band frequency classifier over sorted occurrence dates
Gap-band frequency classifier over sorted occurrence dates
Title
docs.text: Gap-band frequency classifier over sorted occurrence dates

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The detector classifies a group's cadence by counting the gaps between consecutive occurrence dates and matching them against four non-overlapping bands, most-specific first.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Implementation of the cadence bar in the candidacy rule. The detector sorts a group's occurrence dates and computes the day-gaps between consecutive dates. Each candidate frequency owns a band of acceptable gap sizes — weekly 5–9 days, biweekly 11–17, monthly 26–38, yearly 360–372 — and a frequency is accepted when enough of the gaps (min_occurrences minus one, i.e. all consecutive steps for the default bar) fall inside its band. Bands are checked most-specific first, which lets a pattern survive one skipped week: a gap of about fourteen days inside an otherwise weekly streak still classifies the streak as weekly because that gap also fails biweekly's count requirement... in practice the surviving classification comes from the band with enough in-band gaps. No band holding enough gaps means no classification and no proposal. The bands are constants in the store, not configuration.

# src/financials/recurrences.py — lines 261–275
def _classify_frequency(dates: list[date], min_occurrences: int) -> str | None:
  """Classify sorted dates by their gap bands (weekly 5-9, biweekly 11-17,
  monthly 26-38, yearly 360-372); None when no band holds enough gaps.
  Non-overlapping bands, checked most-specific first — a skipped week
  (gap ≈ 14) inside a weekly streak still classifies weekly."""
  gaps = [(b - a).days for a, b in zip(dates, dates[1:], strict=False)]
  for frequency, lo, hi in (
    ("weekly", 5, 9),
    ("biweekly", 11, 17),
    ("monthly", 26, 38),
    ("yearly", 360, 372),
  ):
    if len([g for g in gaps if lo <= g <= hi]) >= min_occurrences - 1:
      return frequency
  return None

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: After each member commits, the membership file is reloaded and the group looked up again before re-pointing the member id — the group store is the mutable baseline, not the loop's copy.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The group-confirm loop cannot carry its own working copy of the membership across iterations: each member's commit may re-read the journal and the group file may have been re-saved by the previous iteration. So after every successful member commit, the group file is loaded anew, the group located again, the member's id replaced by its committed id, and the file saved. This restarts from the actual file each time, which is also why a member disappearing mid-loop (resolve failure) is tolerated — the resolution is against the latest state, whatever earlier iterations changed.

def cmd_delete(target: str, journal: Journal | None = None) -> tuple[Mutation, bool]:
  """Append a delete carrying the victim's full pre-image (read from
  the live ledger BEFORE the append) and apply it. Returns (mutation,
  deleted) — False when the target is unknown (nothing appended)."""
  journal = journal or command_journal()
  ledger = load_ledger(journal)
  victim, _ = ledger.find(target)
  if victim is None:
    return DeleteMutation(  # nothing appended: nothing happened
      date=Date("1970-01-01"),
      description="",
      category="",
      postings={},
      target=target,
    ), False
  mutation = DeleteMutation(
    date=victim.date,
    description=victim.description,
    category=victim.category,
    postings=dict(victim.postings),
    linked=list(victim.linked),
    target=target,
  )
  append_and_apply(mutation, journal)
  return mutation, True

@dataclass
class DeleteMutation(Mutation):
  """Delete = the victim's full pre-image + target id. date/description/
  category/postings/linked are the VICTIM's content at deletion time
  (the pre-image), not the deletion's own execution data. The fold
  verifies the pre-image against the live row before reversing: a
  mismatch stops loudly (the journal claims a delete that does not
  match reality — replaying it silently would corrupt the chain). One
  line therefore reconstructs the deleted item AND proves it deleted
  the right thing."""

docs.text: Every rule command reads the whole rule file into rule objects, changes the in-memory list, and rewrites the entire file with every rule serialized as a data-field row, two-space indented. docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The sweep globs the pending names, sorts them, applies each, then renames the file with its extension doubled by the suffix; nothing reads the applied names again.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The bulk sweep's state machine is entirely in file names. Pending files match the fixed name stem with a json or toml extension; applied ones match with the doubled suffix and never match the pending glob again. Application is sequential, oldest name first; the rename happens only after a file's fixes complete, and a failing file keeps its pending name. This is why 'all pending' is idempotent across crash windows and why a failed file self-retries on the next run.

The confirm commit is an add mutation carrying the retired plan id
Title
docs.text: The confirm commit is an add mutation carrying the retired plan id

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The commit core calls the ordinary booking builder with the plan id in the retire list, which selects the confirm-flavored mutation; applying it inserts the row with the retired ids in its linked list.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The confirmation runs on the same machinery as every booking. The commit core builds the booking through the shared command builder, passing the plan's id in the retire list; that presence switches the builder from a plain add mutation to the confirm flavor at the journal level. Applying it walks the ledger: it finds its date position, inserts the transaction with the plan id recorded on the linked list beside itself, computes the category postings and propagates running balances forward. The mutation is stamped and appended to the journal first, so the books cannot apply what the journal does not record, and the register strike happens only after the apply returns a committed row. The register write is a full list rewrite that keeps every row except the confirmed one.

@dataclass
class ConfirmMutation(AddMutation):
  op: str = field(default="confirm", init=False)

  def apply_on(self, ledger: "Ledger") -> Transaction | None:
    existing, _ = ledger.find(self.id or "")
    if existing:  # idempotent re-apply
      return existing
    return ledger.insert(
      Transaction(
        id=self.id,
        date=self.date,
        description=self.description,
        category=self.category,
        postings=self.postings,
        linked=[*self.retires, *self.linked],

  def insert(self, transaction: Transaction) -> Transaction:
    """
    idx      0     1          2        3     4     5
    before   Z   parent       X        Y     Z
    after    Z   parent  transaction   X     Y     Z
    """
    parent, idx = self.find_parent(transaction.date)
    balances = parent.balances if parent else {}
    transaction.balances = self.apply_postings(balances, transaction.postings)
    transaction.rehash()
    self.transactions.insert(idx + 1, transaction)
    self.propagate(transaction.postings, idx + 2)
    return transaction
