Title
docs.text: The edit-confirm rides the add mutation carrying the retired plan id

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The confirm-from-edit path appends a confirm mutation (an add that retires the plan's id) and strikes the expected row only after the booking applied successfully.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Implementation account of the confirm-from-edit rule. The path builds one mutation through the shared add route — with the plan's id attached as the retired plan — appends and applies it through the single write step, and finds the booked entry by the mutation's id. Only after the booking succeeded is the plan row dropped from the expected register (re-saving it without the row). This ordering is the business guarantee: the strike never precedes a successful booking. If the booking fails (no predecessor row), the plan survives untouched and the bookkeeper is told the conversion did not happen. The linked reference rides along: the new transaction's linked list carries the retired plan id, so the booking remains provably tied to the plan it replaced.

The instance id is a content hash of rule and occurrence
Title
docs.text: The instance id is a content hash of rule and occurrence

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A rule instance's identity is derived by hashing the rule's defining values with its occurrence date — which is why an edited rule re-mints ids and old ids stop resolving.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Rule instances have no home of their own: their identifier is computed from the rule's description, category, amount and the occurrence date, so two viewings of the same due date produce the same id and any edit to the rule's values produces a different one. The confirm and view paths therefore always resolve instance ids freshly from today's rules — a previously displayed id can stop resolving after a rule edit, and the confirm-id window determines which occurrences are reachable at all.

# src/financials/recurrences.py — lines 128–146
def instance_id(rule: Recurrence, occurrence: date) -> str:
  """The virtual instance's content-hash id — deterministic, the SAME
  16-hex scheme as committed rows (with an r: provenance prefix so the
  virtual nature stays visible at a glance). Same rule instance -> same
  id across invocations; editing the RULE changes future instances' ids
  (the id is the manifestation's content, as the owner designed)."""
  payload = {
    "date": occurrence.isoformat(),
    "description": rule.description,
    "category": rule.category,
    "amount": rule.amount,
    "frequency": rule.frequency,
    "day": rule.day,
    "month": rule.month,
  }
  canonical = json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False, sort_keys=True)
  return "r:" + hashlib.sha256(canonical.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]

docs.title: The update replays as delete plus insert composing two balance primitives
The update replays as delete-plus-insert composing two balance primitives
Title
docs.text: The update replays as delete-plus-insert composing two balance primitives

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Applying an update mutation removes the old row with reversed postings and reinserts the replacement at its date position, so balances re-derive through both primitives' propagation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Implementation account of the full-replacement rule. The applied update mutation looks up the target row and composes Transaction.update, which is defined as delete-plus-insert. The delete step removes the row and un-does its postings on every later day (each later row's balances adjusted by the reversed amounts and rehashed). The insert step positions the replacement after the last row dated on or before the new date, recomputes its balances from the predecessor, and propagates the new postings forward through every subsequent row. Because the entry's id rides along unchanged, references held elsewhere — for instance a confirmation that retired a plan id — stay resolvable; balances are never stored as state but re-derived each time. Two guards along the way — the update on an unknown id does nothing and returns nothing, which the journal replay treats as idempotence.

  def update(self, update: Transaction) -> Transaction | None:
    """Update = delete + insert: the two balance-correct primitives,
    composed. The transaction's id (assigned at creation) rides along,
    so linked references elsewhere stay valid; balances re-derive
    through the propagation of both steps."""
    assert update.id is not None
    if not self.delete(update.id):
      return None
    return self.insert(update)

def append_and_apply(mutation: Mutation, journal: Journal | None = None) -> Ledger:
  """THE single write step: stamp ts, append the mutation, boot the
  ledger (checkpoint + tail replay — the just-appended mutation rides
  the tail), and persist the converged checkpoint. Returns the live
  ledger for feedback (find the applied entry by mutation id)."""
  journal = journal or command_journal()
  if not mutation.ts:
    mutation.ts = next(_clock)
  if not mutation.id:
    mutation.id = mutation.content_hash
  journal.append(mutation)
  ledger = load_ledger(journal)
  checkpoint(journal)
  return ledger

docs.text:
Journal-native command mutations (roadmap step 6): every mutating command (add / edit / delete / fixes) builds a mutation, appends it to the canonical journal, and persists the checkpoint. There is no intermediate store: the journal IS the store of record, the ledger's engine owns balance chaining and date ordering, and ledger.json is the snapshot the next boot hydrates from.

Mutation ids are content hashes (one hash scheme end-to-end); machine paths stamp a monotonic ts so identical content still yields distinct ids (the Q8 lesson). Confirm an open entry in one step (financials confirm).

The fast path for the view's OPEN section: a landed-but-unconfirmed expected row (e####) or rule instance (r:-hash) is committed into the journaled ledger with the zero-prompt idiom — the stored values are taken as-is, no field prompts. The adjust path stays 'edit ' (prefilled prompts); a wrong confirm is recoverable via delete/edit, and the commit is journaled either way.

Resolver chain (same shape as edit/delete, exact ids only): t#### (committed hash) -> already actual: idempotent no-op (exit 0) e#### (expected) -> ConfirmMutation retires the e-row and the actual lands in one mutation; the expected row is dropped only after the confirm applied r:-hash (rule instance) -> AddMutation with the rule's own values; a covering commit supersedes the instance automatically, a drifted one is excepted Bare 'confirm' shows the OPEN section (the confirmation backlog) and asks which row to confirm. Anything unresolvable exits 2 with the standard 'Onbekende id' message.

Change-set engine (roadmap step 6): apply reviewed fix files against the journaled ledger.

The change-set is an in-memory list of dicts (the internal contract); financials fix --file loads a JSON/TOML document and routes it through this engine. Field ops re-point at the committed ledger: each op becomes one UpdateMutation carrying the target's FINAL row state (idempotent, final-state semantics — the from-guard still prevents stale edits from clobbering newer values). remove_row emits a DeleteMutation targeting the victim's journal id (pre-image from the ledger). add_expected_row and e-targeted remove_row keep operating on the expected register (hypotheticals, overlay — never committed facts).

Every mutation is applied through the single write step (commands.append_and_apply): append → boot (replay) → checkpoint. A guard violation aborts BEFORE any append, so every journal line records a change that actually happened.

docs.text:
Groups: named rollups of projected/committed rows (financials group).

A group bundles related rows into one virtual row in the view — the credit-card statement case: every purchase of one statement is a member (e####, committed hash id, or r: rule instance) and the statement shows as a single "Mastercard" row with the summed amount on the payment date.

Groups are organization metadata, NOT money movement: they are not journaled (journal = committed money; expected + rules + groups = forecast inputs), they live in their own groups.json overlay, and membership edits never touch the member rows themselves. The projection is a VIEW: hiding members and rolling them up happens at render/walk time, and a group's members keep their ids — group add/remove only edits the membership list.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
Journal (append-only mutations) + ledger (applied transactions).

Identity vs integrity (decided 2026-09-18, docs/journaled-ledger.md): - a MUTATION's id IS its anti-corruption validator: 16-hex content hash over the canonical mutation minus the id (rehash on read) - a TRANSACTION's id is assigned ONCE by its creating mutation (add | confirm) and never recomputed — updates and balance propagation keep it, so linked/retires never need scanning - a transaction carries a separate stored hash (content hash minus the hash field, balances included) guarding its row on disk; recomputed by every writer (insert, update, propagate) - identical mutation content needs distinct ids (two Q8 rows): every mutation carries ts (creation time, hashed content) so content hashes never collide between two real entries Ops: add | update | delete | confirm — no opening op (openings are ordinary add transactions; the first posting to an account creates it).

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
Quick-add shorthand parser for financials add "...".

Grammar (left to right, whitespace-separated): [date] [amount] [Category:]description

  • date: ISO (2026-09-12), vandaag/today, morgen/tomorrow, overmorgen, gisteren/yesterday, eergisteren, or ±Nd relative days (e.g. -3d). Relative days REQUIRE the d suffix — bare "-25" is always an amount.
  • amount: signed (+/-) or currency-marked (€/eur) number, comma decimal allowed, 0 rejected. A bare unsigned number is NEVER an amount — it stays part of the description ("25 jaar jubileum" keeps its text).
  • rest: description, optionally "Category: description" where Category case-insensitively matches an approved category.

Anything omitted is prompted afterwards by the caller (date defaults to today via Enter); nothing is ever silently assumed.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
The TUI's step-3 add dialog: a native Textual form (modal screen) for financials tui's a key.

One source of truth for the RULES: validation, projection and the save mutations are imported from the CLI modules (entry._validate / _validate_amount, commands.projected_checking / cmd_add, expected.add_expected) — only the PROMPTING is native widgets. The same dispatch as the CLI applies: a future date saves to the expected register instead of the journal (no balance chaining — expected rows have no balances), and the CLI's future-date rejection inside entry._validate is bypassed by dispatching BEFORE it (CLI parity: entry.add_transaction dispatches before _validate too).

Form: Datum / Omschrijving / Categorie / Bedrag / checking-saldo confirmation. Enter walks the fields (Tab works natively too); on the saldo field Enter submits. Esc cancels (dismiss(None)).

The category is a FUZZY AUTOCOMPLETE (textual-autocomplete), not free text: the approved categories (config-driven, call time) are offered in a dropdown the moment the field takes focus — an empty input shows ALL of them (questionary-style), typing narrows fuzzily. Enter completes the highlighted match and advances to the next field (the library intercepts Enter/Tab while the dropdown is visible; a mouse click completes too). Esc with the dropdown open only hides it — a second Esc cancels the dialog. Enter on a hidden dropdown accepts an EXACT approved category; anything else is refused inline (submit re-validates every value, so a Tab-past is caught at the gate too). A bare 'q' in any field cancels (CLI parity).

The saldo confirmation shows the live projection for the typed date+amount; blank accepts the projection (the data-quality gate is "you saw the number", the typed value is never stored — balances are engine-computed). Enter-driven — no per-keystroke ledger boots.

Tests: pilot-pressable. Validation errors render inline (a Static line) instead of rich console output.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
The TUI (steps 1–3): a scrollable ledger view — Textual App + DataTable, consuming build_view (the same composition as list; one composition, two renderers) — the step-2 readonly detail dialog, and the step-3 add dialog (a, implemented in tui/add.py).

Keys: up/down (j/k) move the row cursor one row; pageup/pagedown by page; home/end jump to the first/last row; q or escape quits; a opens the add dialog; enter opens the detail dialog on an entry row. The DataTable clamps at the first/last row by itself (no offset math here) and auto-scrolls the viewport when the cursor reaches a screen edge. The table holds the FULL committed history above the actuals window; the initial view is positioned on the projection: the PROJECTIE row at the bottom of the viewport with the 10 rows above it starting at the top, so the forecast's near future is what you see first.

Row design: every entry row is TWO lines tall — the Datum column holds the date; the merged second column holds the id (line 1, dim) and "description / category" (line 2); the amount and the two balances are their own single-line columns. Section separators stay one line (label in the merged column). The merged column FILLS: the other columns stay content-sized and it takes every remaining cell (fit_columns — DataTable has no flex columns), so the numbers end flush at the right edge. Rows are mixed-height (add_row height=2); only the initial-position scroll math needs line offsets — cursor, keys and dialogs stay row-based.

Step 2: Enter on an entry row opens the readonly DetailScreen (the row's full data + a provenance status line); Esc/q closes it. The screen composes from the entry tuple so the editable step reuses it.

Step 3: a opens the AddScreen form (native widgets; the validation and save rules are imported from the CLI modules). On save the table rebuilds from a fresh build_view and the cursor lands on the newly added row; a toast confirms the new id.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
One-time bootstrap for the journaled ledger (roadmap step 1).

See docs/journaled-ledger.md. Reads the current stores and emits, into a STAGING directory (default: /migration — never the live store root, never overwriting existing outputs without --force):

events.jsonl append-only journal: two opening events (seed balances, derived from the first row) + one committed event per actual row, in replay order; NO sequence numbers — the row order IS the order. id = 16-hex content hash over the canonical event minus id (self-validating, idempotent appends, deterministic bootstrap) ledger.json checkpoint: folded entries + computed balances + tip (id of the last journal event — the watermark) expected.json pruned hypotheticals (balances and source_line stripped) rules.json recurrences, carried as-is (they never had balances)

Seed rule (decided 2026-09-18): opening = first row's recorded balance minus that row's own effect on the account. Worked example t0001 (2024-11-24, Huur, +350,00, recorded 3.126,47 / 20.000,00): checking opening = 3126.47 - 350.00 = 2776.47 savings opening = 20000.00 (no transfer in the first row)

Op vocabulary (final): add | update | delete | confirm. No opening op (openings are ordinary add mutations: "Opening", Inkomsten); no reconcile op — money that moved without a transaction becomes an explicit correction TRANSACTION (owner policy 2026-09-18: "I will always create a transaction implementing the mutation"); the bootstrap derives those correction rows and lists them for review.

Every mutation carries ts (creation time, part of the hashed content): identical content then yields DISTINCT ids (two Q8 rows stay two rows — the 2026-09-19 duplicate-collapse incident). Machine-minted rows get a monotonic clock (never repeats); human entries rely on manual distinctness. Ids are minted through journal.py's Mutation classes, so bootstrap and engine share one hash scheme.

Verification gate (two-tier): HARD: the folded TIP must equal the recorded tip — the one comparison that validates the entire amount chain end-to-end. On failure: report, exit non-zero, write NOTHING. SOFT: per-row balance deviations are counted and shown; after the correction pass this must be EMPTY — any survivor is an inconsistency between corrections and the fold.

Run by the owner (Makefile target: migration-boostrap): uv run python scripts/bootstrap_journal.py

docs.text:
One-time data promotion (roadmap step 6, phase D1–D6).

Moves the migration staging stores to their canonical locations and retires the old stores — renamed with a timestamp, never destroyed. After this, command_journal() resolves to /journal.jsonl (the staging file no longer exists) and the app boots from the promoted stores with no further change.

Moves (in order, rollback = copy the backups back): D1 data/journal.jsonl -> backups/journal.jsonl.retired- (old audit trail) D4 migration/journal.jsonl -> data/journal.jsonl (the event journal) migration/ledger.json -> data/ledger.json (its checkpoint) D2 data/transactions.json -> backups/transactions.json.retired- D3 data/expected.json -> backups/expected.json.retired- migration/expected.json -> data/expected.json (pruned baseline) D5 migration/rules.json deleted ONLY when byte-identical to data/recurrences.json (which stays put); refusal otherwise D6 migration/ removed when empty

Guards: - pre-flight: the staging journal folds cleanly and its tip is recorded; the same tip must hold after the move (the move is byte-preserving) - expected.json drift check: any row present in the LIVE store but missing from the staging baseline REFUSES the promotion loudly (rows added after the bootstrap would be lost) — the owner decides - post-verify: load_ledger() from the promoted location == the pre-flight fold (ids + balances)

Run (Makefile target: migration-promote): uv run python scripts/promote_stores.py # dry-run: report only uv run python scripts/promote_stores.py --write # backups + move + verify

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
One-time regeneration: rewrite the staging checkpoint to the canonical fold (roadmap step 6 boot requirement).

Why: the staged migration/ledger.json was written by the bootstrap's file-order evidence pass (step 1). Step 3 made the engine's date-positioned fold THE canonical fold (design note, 2026-09-21), so the staged checkpoint's ROW ORDER is stale wherever a journal row's date differs from its file position (the 47 known inversion rows). Balances are fine (tip holds: unchanged from the bootstrap) — only the order is stale, but load_ledger hydrates rows as persisted, so a stale order boots the ledger in non-date order until a tail replay re-derives it. This script folds the journal canonically and persists the result atomically.

Run (Makefile target: migration-recheckpoint): uv run python scripts/recheckpoint.py # dry-run: report only uv run python scripts/recheckpoint.py --write # backup + rewrite + verify

Verification gate: after writing, hydration from the new checkpoint must equal a fresh fold exactly (ids + balances), and the tip balances must hold at the bootstrap values.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
One-time repair: re-mint stale mutation ids in the migration journal.

The step-2 observer bug (2026-09-19): four live confirm rows were appended by a writer that stamped ts into the journal line but minted the id over content WITHOUT ts. The id doubles as the row's anti-corruption validator (16-hex content hash over the canonical mutation minus the id), so those rows now fail fold()'s rehash verification — the fold refuses loudly.

This script scans the journal, re-derives the id from each mismatched row's own content (the content itself is never touched), and rewrites ONLY the affected lines. Everything else stays byte-identical.

Run (Makefile target: migration-remint): uv run python scripts/remint_journal_ids.py # dry-run: report only uv run python scripts/remint_journal_ids.py --write # backup + repair + verify

Verification gate: after writing, the full journal must fold cleanly (at the bootstrap tip balances); the script refuses to write when the scan finds nothing, and reports loudly when the post-fold check fails.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
Shared test fixtures: journal + expected-store isolation.

Every test runs with the canonical journal resolved through financials.fixes.journal_file pointed at a temporary directory — so running the suite never appends to the owner's real journal — and with the expected store pointed at a tmp file too: fix flows legitimately READ the expected register (e.g. add_expected_row's id-uniqueness check), and reading the owner's real store would make tests depend on live data (or crash on its row shape). A test that wants the live stores overrides these fixtures explicitly.

The rollup is the display unit: build_view seats it into the actuals AT the chain position of the last member in chain order (the point where the total landed) — the renderer places nothing; whatever sits after it (e.g. Bankkosten committed after the members) renders below the rollup, exactly as the ledger orders it. The TUI's history band keeps its own pre-window rollup placement in view.rollups.

docs.title: Process story — Entry removal
docs.text:
process-story · for client

A double recording, a card payment logged twice, a plan no longer expected — the bookkeeper opens the delete command and names the row, or lets it show the last ten past rows and picks from that menu. The typed id is resolved in exactly one place, consulted in strict order: the committed books first, then the planned-entry register, then the row groupings, then the projected occurrences of recurring rules. Nothing is removed without a typed affirmative — bare Enter, an unknown word or an interruption all leave every store untouched. An actual transaction's removal is itself a recorded event: it joins the append-only history carrying the row's complete content as it stood, read from the live books before anything changes, and at every later read-back that stored snapshot is checked against the books — a mismatch stops the books from opening at all rather than letting the history claim a removal it did not make, and the balances of every later row are re-carried so no drift remains. Removing a transfer earns an extra warning, because the savings side moved too. The planning stores keep no such history: a plan is simply struck from its register, a rule occurrence is suppressed by adding its date to the rule's exceptions so the rule keeps running for its other periods, and a grouping dissolves without touching its member rows. There is no undo — a wrongly removed entry is re-recorded anew; the journal is the audit trail of what was taken off the books.

docs.title: Process story — Entry revision
docs.text:
process-story · for client

A typo in the amount, a moved date, a miscategorized spend — the bookkeeper names the entry or picks from the last ten dated-upto-today rows, reads the row as it stands, and walks one pre-filled pass over date, description, category and amount: Enter keeps a value, re-typing it is the change, and only real changes are recorded. A wiped description abandons the whole session without storing anything, and an id that names nothing is refused. Where the correction lands follows the new date. A recorded entry corrected to today or earlier becomes one journaled event that restates the row in full — every later day's running balance is re-derived from it, so the books stay truthful from that day onward. A recorded entry corrected into the future leaves the books: the row is removed first and re-created as a plan second, a deliberate sequencing that names the recovery path when the parking fails — and for a transfer the bookkeeper is warned to check the savings side. A plan edited toward today or the past books itself into the ledger and leaves the register only after the booking succeeded; accepting every field unchanged on a plan that already landed is confirmation by itself. A plan that stays in the future is simply rewritten where it sits.

docs.title: Process story — Ledger cleanup change-set application
docs.text:
process-story · for client

Mistakes that predate the tool — or corrections reviewed away from the machine — arrive as small change-set files: each fix names one ledger row and what should change about it, a corrected field possibly guarded by the old value it expects, or a whole-row action such as striking the row or clearing a parked plan. The fix command takes one reviewed file or sweeps every pending file oldest first. Every fix is checked against the live books before it applies: the row must be known and unambiguous, a stated old value must still match, and a removal's captured content must equal the live row. A fix that passes becomes exactly one recorded change — the record carries the corrected row in full, the books rebook the row and re-derive every later running balance. A refused fix stops the run at that fix: the message names the row, the field and the two disagreeing values, everything earlier in the file stays applied, nothing afterward applies and the file keeps its name until repaired. When a file's fixes all land, it is renamed with an applied marker so it can never run twice. Plans are not part of the books, so a removal aimed at a parked plan clears the register directly, with no recorded change. The change journal is the durable account of what actually reached the books.

docs.title: Process story — Confirmation of landed plans
docs.text:
process-story · for client

The rent or insurance that existed only as a plan has now landed at the bank; the bookkeeper confirms it in one step and is asked nothing — the planned figure commits as it was recorded, because adjusting values is the edit door's job, done beforehand. The confirmation books the money through the same doors as any manual booking, and only after the booking succeeds is the plan struck from the register — a refused confirmation (a plan still dated ahead, or carrying no amount) changes nothing, and an already-settled id is answered with a nothing-to-do note, so repeated confirming can never double-book. A due instance of a recurring rule commits from the rule's own values; if the real booking drifted beyond tolerance, the occurrence is noted as an exception date on the rule so the stale forecast line quietly leaves. A group of landed plans walks its members in date order — the group survives, and members that are still future or amountless are skipped with notes rather than blocking the rest. What the household gains: planned money becomes recorded money, the plan registers shrink, and the journal carries proof of which plan each payment settled.

docs.title: Process story — Recurring payment provisioning
docs.text:
process-story · for client

The same bill arrives month after month, and the bookkeeper asks the tool to scan the committed history for it: patterns where description and category repeat at regular spacing and occur often enough. The answer is a review table of candidate rules — and the tool's own promise that nothing has been created. Each proposal carries the detected pattern, including the honest low-to-high range when amounts vary. Taking a proposal opens the field-by-field editor seeded with those values: the bookkeeper keeps or overwrites each, the same validation every recording meets applies, and only then does the rule enter the store. From that moment the rule works invisibly for the forecast: each due date projects a virtual occurrence into the view until real money in the books covers it. The rule can be paused and resumed unchanged, re-edited, or retired — retirement takes a typed confirmation and erases only the rule, never the history that detected it. The forecast layer never touches the books; only the bookkeeper's later explicit confirmation of a due occurrence turns projected money into recorded money.

docs.title: Process story — Transaction intake
docs.text:
process-story · for client

A spend happens, or comes to mind too late — the bookkeeper opens the add surface and gives the details as a one-line quick-add or through prompts that ask for anything missing. Nothing is assumed: the date must parse, the description must be there, the category must sit on the household's approved list, and the amount must be non-zero when the movement is real. On the prompted path the books themselves join the session: the bookkeeper sees what the checking balance will read after this entry and must confirm it — three mismatches and the whole recording is thrown away, so a mis-keyed figure dies as a cancelled session rather than a wrong balance. A one-line quick-add skips that balance gate. Then the date decides: an entry dated ahead is kept as tomorrow's plan — balance-free, and an empty amount is allowed as a deliberate placeholder — while a past or same-day movement is posted to the books: stamped with its own identity, filed in the append-only history, and every later day's running balance carried forward so the position stays truthful down the chain. The bookkeeper hears the saved entry's id and the new balances; every refusal or interrupted session along the way leaves nothing stored.

docs.title: Archetype mapping
docs.text:
archetype-mapping · for client

The archetype is a double-entry-adjacent personal ledger with a forecast layer: a single-household bookkeeping suite that keeps an auditable account of committed money, a parking place for planned money, and a rules engine that turns history into forecast — nothing cloud-served, no multi-user world, just one household's two accounts kept provably true. Four core concepts carry the whole shape.

Actual versus expected is the load-bearing distinction: a movement either happened (dated today or earlier) and lives in the journaled books, or it is planned (dated ahead) and parks in a register that carries no balances. Nearly every rule and boundary in the project reads as a consequence of that one line.

Content-hash identity is the integrity archetype: a recording's identity is a hash of its own content plus creation time, appended to a journal that can never be edited — so the books replay their own history rather than remember it.

Running balances is the everyday payoff: every ledger row carries the balance it produced, so the household position at any date is a read, not a recalculation, and a backdated entry threads itself into the chain and pushes every later balance truthful again.

The approved category list is budgeting policy made executable — the household's own configured vocabulary is checked fresh at every recording on both the actual and the expected side.

Two further concepts organize the planner: a rule instance is a projected, virtual occurrence — real in the forecast, never in the books — and the confirmation backlog names what has landed but not yet been confirmed, one queue with one drain path.

How the concepts live in the components, in the component census's own order:

  • The transaction entry interface is where actual-versus-expected is policed at the front door — it validates, routes by date, and closes the loop with the projected-balance confirmation.
  • The confirmation dispatcher is the only bridge between the two worlds: it commits known values as recorded money without a conversation.
  • The interactive entry editor moves entries across that boundary by their corrected date — future edits turn recorded rows into plans, past-dated plans book into the ledger.
  • The recurrence engine is the forecast layer proper: rule store, projection of virtual instances, and the detection that proposes rules — never writing money itself.
  • The interactive deletion dispatcher is the four-way resolver: each store owns its own removal path, and destructive steps demand a typed affirmative.
  • The journaled ledger engine realizes content-hash identity and running balances — append, replay, verify, carry balances forward.
  • The expected register store is the planned-money world: strictly future-dated, balance-free, struck the moment a plan settles.
  • The cleanup fix engine treats corrections as reviewed, offline-authored change-set files (the change-set concept), each fix guarded — a fix may state the old value the ledger must confirm, the from-guard.

Basis note: this story rests on a deterministic sample of 12 of 17 concept facts, with all 17 censused; the 8 components were read in full.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
executive-summary · for client

It is a household ledger — the archetype story calls it a double-entry-adjacent personal ledger with a forecast layer — and its whole design protects one thing: books that can prove their own history.

  1. The books replay their own history: every change joins an append-only, content-hashed journal — timestamped so even identical same-day recordings stay distinct — and every row re-verifies on read; a correction is a new recorded event, never a quiet edit.
  2. Planned money cannot corrupt recorded money: recurring rules and their forecast are an overlay never materialized into the books, and the only bridge from plan to reality is the deliberately zero-prompt confirm of a landed entry.
  3. A caution for bulk-cleanup reviews: an amount correction on a transfer row silently overwrites any custom savings side — a reviewer fixing one field should expect both sides to rewrite.
  4. Destructive actions demand a typed affirmative and offer no undo; the journal — not a restore command — is the recovery story.

Verification status: no objection facts and no verification-phase records exist in the fact base at narration time, so these findings rest on the analyst passes' own confidence.

Next step: read the companion product summary and archetype mapping for the capability walk and concept map, then the per-surface detail sections.

docs.title: Product summary
docs.text:
product-summary · for client

This is a household bookkeeping suite: typed commands over one household's checking and savings money, built so the books can always prove what was done to them. Everything rides one distinction — money that happened versus money that is only planned — and every capability below keeps that line sharp.

Recording a movement is the front door. The bookkeeper gives a spend or income as a one-line quick-add or through prompts that ask for anything missing; date, description, an approved category and a signed amount are checked — the category must be on the household's approved list — and the entry routes by its date: any future-dated entry parks in the expected register instead of the actual books, while moving money between the household's own accounts touches both balances at once. On the prompted path the balance is part of the deal: the projected checking balance is confirmed before anything saves, three mismatches throw the recording away, and no hand-corrected balance can ever be stored.

Confirming landed plans is the second door. When planned money arrives — a parked one-off entry, a due instance of a recurring rule, or a group of them — one confirm step commits the planned values with no questions asked, strikes the plan from the register, and answers an already-settled id harmlessly so nothing double-books. Adjusting values is deliberately the edit surface's job, done before confirming — never the confirm's.

Correcting walks one pre-filled form — Enter keeps a field, re-typing changes it, and only real changes are recorded. Where the correction lands follows the new date: a recorded entry corrected to today or earlier is journaled as a full restatement so later balances stay truthful; a recorded entry pushed into the future leaves the books and becomes a plan; a plan edited into the past books itself without further questions.

Recurring payments become standing rules. The tool scans the committed history for regularly repeating patterns, proposes them as read-only review rows — detection never creates a rule — and stores a rule only after the bookkeeper approves each detected field. An approved rule projects virtual due-dates into the forecast; it pauses, resumes, edits or retires without ever touching the books. The forecast is an overlay; only the bookkeeper's explicit confirmation of a due date creates recorded money.

Removing an entry is deliberate and loud. A typed id resolves in exactly one store — books, register, groups or rule occurrences — the row is shown, and a typed affirmative is required; bare Enter cancels. An actual transaction's removal is itself journal-recorded with its complete prior content, so history stays provable; the design offers no undo — re-creating a wrongly removed entry means recording it anew.

The books themselves are the spine: every business change joins an append-only journal as a mutation stamped with a creation time and a content hash, replayed into a ledger that carries each row's running balance and re-verifies every row on read. The household always sees the balance a recording produces, at any date, without recalculation.

Bulk corrections travel as reviewed change-set files: each fix names one known row, may state the old value it expects, and lands as exactly one recorded change; pending files sweep oldest first and are renamed applied when consumed. Cleanup can correct or trim history — it can never add rows to the actual books.

Where the product stops is design, not omission: balances are never hand-overridden at saving time, intake never asks for subcategories, confirmation never adjusts values, committed removals have no undo, and no automatic step ever writes recorded money on its own.

One honesty note on basis: the rule citations above rest on a deterministic sample of 12 of 60 business-rule facts, with all 60 censused; components, non-goals and processes were read in full.

Title
docs.text: A cleanup change-set never adds rows to the actual books

docs.title: Non-Goal Statement
docs.text: The whole-row action set a cleanup file may use contains only removal of recorded rows, clearing of parked plans and parking of new planned entries — no action introduces a new row into the actual books.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Cleanup is subtractive or corrective; new recorded movements enter the books only through the ordinary entry flows, never via a fix file.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A fix file can correct a row's fields or strike a row, and it can park a planned entry into the expected register (also a route for the interactive flows' internal ops list). It cannot create a new recorded transaction: no row-adding action exists in the change-set vocabulary, and the row engine refuses any action name outside its set. The boundary keeps cleanup files from becoming a second entry path — recorded history grows only at the entry interface, while cleanup only fixes or trims it.

Non-Goal Statement
docs.text: The one-step confirm never prompts for date, description, category or amount of a landed plan; the interactive adjustments only exist on the separate future-instance path, not as an option of the landed confirm.

docs.title: Confirming writes no per instance store
Non-Goal Statement
docs.text: Confirming a rule instance does not materialize or store the instance anywhere — only the ordinary booking exists after the commit, plus possibly an exception date on the rule.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The recurrence model stays projection-only through confirmation — no rows are minted per instance, the rule file gains at most one exception date.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The recurrence design keeps instances virtual: they are projected from rules for display, never stored as rows. Confirmation respects that boundary — the confirm books real money and never records "this instance was confirmed" except through the booking itself (and, when the booking drifted, an exception date on the rule so the stale projection leaves). docs.title: No undo for a committed removal
No undo for a committed removal
Non-Goal Statement
docs.text: The books deliberately offer no undo of a committed removal — the journal's audit trail is the only record of what was removed, and no command reverses it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A removed transaction is gone from the ledger view for good — the design point is that the journal records the removal, not that an undo restores it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The delete module's docstring states the boundary plainly — there is no undo; the journal is the audit trail of what was removed. Re-creating a wrongly removed transaction means adding it again as a new entry, not restoring the old one. This is a deliberate design choice, not an oversight — the removal record with its full pre-image is the recoverability story. The household that wants an entry back re-enters it; the journal stays append-only in both directions.

# src/financials/delete.py — lines 1–11
"""Delete an existing transaction or expected entry (financials delete).

Resolves the id in the committed ledger (hash id, full or unambiguous
prefix) or the expected register (e####), shows the row, and requires an
explicit confirmation (bare Enter is NOT yes). Actual rows are applied
as one DeleteMutation carrying the victim's full pre-image (the engine
verifies it against the live row and refuses loudly on mismatch).
Expected rows are removed from the expected register (no balance chain).

There is no undo; the journal IS the audit trail of what was removed.
"""

# src/financials/commands.py — lines 152–176
def cmd_delete(target: str, journal: Journal | None = None) -> tuple[Mutation, bool]:
  """Append a delete carrying the victim's full pre-image (read from
  the live ledger BEFORE the append) and apply it. Returns (mutation,
  deleted) — False when the target is unknown (nothing appended)."""
  journal = journal or command_journal()
  ledger = load_ledger(journal)
  victim, _ = ledger.find(target)
  if victim is None:
    return DeleteMutation(  # nothing appended: nothing happened
      date=Date("1970-01-01"),
      description="",
      category="",
      postings={},
      target=target,
    ), False
  mutation = DeleteMutation(
    date=victim.date,
    description=victim.description,
    category=victim.category,
    postings=dict(victim.postings),
    linked=list(victim.linked),
    target=target,
  )
  append_and_apply(mutation, journal)
  return mutation, True

docs.title: Non-Goal Statement
docs.text: The system deliberately never writes the recurring rules' projected instances into the actual books or any persistent instance store — instances exist only as the view-time projection, until a real booking supersedes or an explicit confirmation books one.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The planner stays an overlay — the design decision that keeps the journal a story of committed money only, stated in the module's own header.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Two boundaries define the rule engine's honesty, both stated as owner decisions in the code's own words. The rule engine's module header: rules are never materialized into the transaction store — instance rows are computed fresh inside each view window and vanish with it. The command surface's header: the rule book is the recurring analogue of the expected register — overlay configuration, not journaled, because the journal is the story of committed money only. Together this means approving a rule, pausing it, or even the forecast showing a due bill never touches the books; only the bookkeeper's explicit confirmation of an instance creates journal entries, through the same doors as any booking. The forecast layer cannot corrupt the ledger by existing.

docs.text:
One business process the analyzed codebase carries out, captured as a process-diagram document with its business trigger — tied to the business rules it realizes and the code that carries the evidence.

Fact Sheet Name Entry removal Entry revision Ledger cleanup-fx application Open-entry confirmation Recurring payment provisioning Transaction intake

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: When an entry turns out not to belong in the books at all, the bookkeeper removes it after explicit confirmation — actual transactions are journaled with their full pre-image so history stays provable, planned entries and rule occurrences are struck from their own planning stores.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A double recording, a card payment logged twice as transactions, a planned entry no longer expected — the bookkeeper opens the delete command and names the row, or lets it show the last ten past rows and picks from that menu. The typed id is resolved in exactly one place: the committed books first (by their content-derived ids), then the planned-entry register, then the grouped-row bundles, then the projected occurrences of recurring rules. Nothing is removed without a typed affirmative — bare Enter, an unknown word and an interruption all leave every store untouched. A committed transaction's removal is itself a recorded event: the removal joins the journal carrying the removed entry's complete content as it stood — date, description, category, its money movements across accounts and its links to other rows — read from the live books before anything changes. At every ledger read-back that stored snapshot is compared with what actually happened in the books, and a mismatch stops the books from opening at all rather than letting the journal silently claim a removal it did not make. The running balances of every later row are re-propagated so no drift remains, and removing a transfer earns an extra warning because the savings chain moved too. The planning stores have no such history: a planned entry is simply struck from the register, a projected rule occurrence is suppressed by adding its date to the rule's exceptions so the rule keeps running for the other periods, and a grouped bundle dissolves without touching its member rows. There is no undo — re-creating a wrongly removed entry means recording it anew; the journal is the audit trail of what was removed. A second door exists for planned entries on the expect surface that strikes without asking — a known deliberation point.

docs.title: Trigger
docs.text: Surface: the financials delete command — a recorded transaction or planned entry must be removed from the books.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The bookkeeper corrects a recorded transaction or a planned entry — a new date, amount, description or category — and every journaled correction re-derives the books afterwards instead of silently rewriting history: a recorded entry's correction rests as a full restatement of its data, an edit into the future turns the recorded entry into a plan, and a landed plan's edit books the plan as it now stands.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A recorded figure turns out to be wrong — a typo'd amount, a moved date, a miscategorized spend — or a planned entry needs its numbers adjusted before the day it lands. The household bookkeeper picks the entry by its id from the list view, or runs the edit bare and picks from the last ten rows (only entries already dated up to today are offered). The editor shows the row as it stands and walks one pass over date, description, category and amount, each field kept by pressing Enter and replaced only by re-typing it. Where the correction lands depends on what the entry is and where its date now falls. A recorded entry corrected to today or earlier is journaled as one event that restates all four of its data values — the books are then re-derived so every later day's running balance stays truthful, and the confirmation line shows the corrected entry with the new checking and savings balances. A recorded entry whose corrected date falls in the future leaves the committed books: it is removed and re-created as a plan at the new date — a sequencing that deliberately removes first, so a failed re-creation leaves the entry in neither store and names the recovery path; for transfers the bookkeeper is warned to check the savings side afterwards. A plan edited toward today or the past is intent to confirm — the plan books into the ledger with its values unchanged or newly edited, and is struck from the register only after the booking succeeded; on a plan that already landed, accepting every field with only Enters is confirmation by itself. A plan that stays in the future is simply rewritten where it sits in the register. Two guardrails shape every session: a wiped description abandons the whole edit without storing anything, and a row carrying no amount at all refuses to be edited. Entries that are actually groups or recurring-plan instances are handed to their own dedicated editors, and an id that names nothing is refused. The correction is provable rather than silent — every journaled route appends an event carrying the full state, so the journal can later show which correction happened and when.

docs.text: A recorded or planned entry contains wrong data and must be corrected (surface: the financials edit command)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Reviewed change-set files containing corrected field values are applied to the journaled ledger oldest-first, each application recorded in an append-only application journal, with the fix files renamed applied when consumed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Historical mistakes that predate the tool — or bulk corrections reviewed offline — arrive as small change-set files: each fix in a file names one ledger row and states what should change about it (a corrected field with an optional old value as a drift guard, or a whole-row action: striking the row, or clearing a parked plan). The household bookkeeper points the fix command at one reviewed file, or lets it sweep every pending file in the data directory, oldest first. For each fix the tool re-reads the live ledger and checks the guards: the row must be known and unambiguous, any stated old value must still match, and a removal's captured content must equal the live row. A fix that passes becomes exactly one recorded change to the books — the appended record carries the corrected row in full, the ledger rebooks the row (remove and re-insert on the same identity) and re-derives every later running balance, then the record's file snapshot converges. A refused fix stops the run at that fix with a message naming row, field and the two disagreeing values: everything earlier in the file stays applied, nothing afterward applies, and the file is not renamed. When all of a file's fixes land, the sweep renames the file with an applied suffix so it never runs twice, and the next file begins. Removals aimed at parked plans clear the register directly — plans are not part of the books, so no recorded change exists for them. The bookkeeper reads the run's table (each fix's outcome beside its stated reason) and repairs any refused file before rerunning; the change journal itself is the durable account of what actually reached the books.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A landed bill or payment that was only planned (expected entry or recurring-rule instance) is confirmed in one step as actually paid; the plan registers are cleaned up and the payment enters the actual ledger as a journaled transaction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A payment the household had only planned — a one-off expected entry or an instance of a recurring rule such as rent or insurance — has now landed at the bank. The bookkeeper confirms it in one step without being asked anything: the planned figure commits as-is, because adjusting values is the edit surface's job done beforehand. For an expected entry the confirmation books the planned values through the same booking doors as any manual recording, carrying the plan's identifier on the committed row so the books prove which plan this payment settled; only then is the plan struck from the expected register, never before a successful booking (a refused confirm — future date or missing amount — removes nothing). For a rule instance the rule's own values commit with no questions and no per-instance record: a booking that still covers the rule's period supersedes the instance silently, while a drifted commit (amount or date moved beyond tolerance) additionally records the occurrence as an exception on the rule so the stale projection leaves the open view. A group confirmation walks the landed members in date order — each commits through its own path, each confirmed plan member is re-pointed to its new committed identifier inside the group's membership, and future, amountless or unresolvable members are skipped with notes while the group itself survives. With no id given, the confirm picker shows the open backlog — everything landed but unconfirmed on or before today — and a single prompt asks which id to confirm; empty input cancels without changing anything. Already-settled identifiers are recognized and answered with a nothing-to-do note, so repeated or over-eager confirming can never double-book. Who perceives it: the household bookkeeper; what changes: planned money becomes recorded money, plan registers shrink, the journal proves the retirement, and the open backlog drains. Traced end to end this engagement: the dispatch (confirm.py confirm_transaction:232), the zero-prompt plan commit (confirm.py _confirm_expected:64, _commit_expected:38), the instance commit core (recurrence_cli.py commit_instance:596) and the group walk (confirm.py _confirm_group:124).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Repeating payments (rent, salary, subscriptions) are detected as candidates from the committed history, reviewed by the bookkeeper, and approved as recurring rules that drive the ledger's forecast.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A recurring payment's life runs from noticing to trusting. The bookkeeper, seeing that the same bill arrives month after month, asks the tool to scan the committed history for patterns — same description and category, regular spacing, occurring often enough. The answer is a review table of candidate rules and the tool's own promise on its foot: nothing has been created. Each proposal carries the detected pattern — description, category, a representative amount (with the honest low-to-high range when amounts vary), the cadence and spacing, and when the pattern started. Taking a proposal opens the field-by-field editor seeded with those values: the bookkeeper keeps or overwrites each, gets the same validation every recording meets, and only then does the rule enter the recurrences store. From that moment the rule works for the forecast invisibly: each due date projects an instance into the view until real money matching the category, amount and timing covers it, or the bookkeeper pauses, re-edits or retires the pattern (pause is reversible; removal takes a typed confirmation and erases only the rule, never the history that made it). The forecast layer never touches the books — rules are an overlay on the journal's story of committed money; only a later explicit confirmation of a due instance creates journal entries. Detection, approval and rule management live in the recurrence commands; the engine's own rules — detection stores nothing, approval saves nothing until the loop completes — make every act here either a review or an explicit, validated write.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The bookkeeper records a spend or income as shorthand or prompted input; a future-dated entry parks in the expected register as a plan, today's or past entry enters the actual ledger as a journaled, hash-verified mutation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The intake of a household money movement, end to end. The household bookkeeper opens the add surface at the moment a spend or income happens or is remembered, giving the details either as a one-line quick-add shorthand or through the prompts; anything missing is asked, nothing is assumed. The surface validates the details — a parseable date, a non-empty description, a category from the household's approved list, a non-zero amount on the actual side — and routes by date: a future entry is handed to the expected register as a parked plan (amount 0 allowed as a deliberate placeholder), a today-or-past entry is posted to the journaled ledger. The posting is a journal-native mutation stamped with a creation time and a content-hash identity, appended to the append-only journal, folded back into the live books with the entry placed at its date position and running balances carried forward through every later row; the converged checkpoint is persisted in the same write pass. The surface echoes the saved id and the resulting balances. Every stop along the way — refusal, aborted prompt, Ctrl-C, three failed balance confirmations — leaves nothing stored. The confirmation gate before saving shows the projected checking balance, derived from the same ledger predecessor the engine will chain from; the bookkeeper confirms it (or retries within three attempts, after which nothing is saved).

docs.title: A covered instance skip inside group confirm checks only the checking posting
A covered-instance skip inside group confirm checks only the checking posting
Title
docs.text: A covered-instance skip inside group confirm checks only the checking posting

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The group path's already-covered test requires the covering booking to touch checking — a savings-only covered booking would not count as covering.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Before committing a rule-instance member of a group, the code checks whether the books already hold a booking that covers the instance (same category, amount within a cent, date inside the window). That check, as spelled there, insists the covering booking carries a checking posting — and only the checking posting's amount is compared to the rule amount. The standalone view's own covering test compares the row's amount without that posting requirement. A rule projected on savings-side movements could therefore be re-committed by a group confirm even though a matching booking already exists on the savings side. In household practice every commit posts to checking, so the difference is latent, but the two covering tests are not the same rule as written.

def _covers(occurrence: date, rule: Recurrence, transactions: list[Transaction]) -> bool:
  """True when a real transaction covers this rule instance's period."""
  window_lo = occurrence - timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  window_hi = occurrence + timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  for t in transactions:
    if not t.date or not t.date.startswith(str(occurrence.year)):
      continue
    t_date = date.fromisoformat(t.date)
    if not (window_lo <= t_date <= window_hi):
      continue
    if t.category != rule.category:
      continue
    if t.amount_eur is None or abs(t.amount_eur - rule.amount) > AMOUNT_TOLERANCE:
      continue
    return True
  return False

docs.title: A rule that already exists is appended again on every approval
A rule that already exists is appended again on every approval
Title
docs.text: A rule that already exists is appended again on every approval

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The add, adopt and edit paths append the new rule without checking whether a rule with the same description and category is already stored — duplicates are possible by hand, never by the detector.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The detector's dedup rule (never re-propose a covered pattern) is the only dedup the flow has. The hand-add path, proposal adoption and even the edit path simply append the (possibly edited) rule object to the loaded list and save — no uniqueness check on description plus category anywhere on the write side. The bookkeeper can therefore store two rules with identical pattern fields by adding twice or by editing a rule's description into another rule's description; both will project their instances into every future period, doubling the forecast. The superseding matcher softens the visual symptom slightly (a covering booking retires one instance of each), but two identical rules stay on the books as two. The collision refusal lives only in the vault, so to speak — not in the store.

docs.title: An amount correction on a transfer row silently overwrites any custom savings side
An amount correction on a transfer row silently overwrites any custom savings side
Title
docs.text: An amount correction on a transfer row silently overwrites any custom savings side

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A transfer row whose savings posting was deliberately set asymmetric gets its savings side rewritten to the exact negative of the new checking amount by any amount correction — with no warning.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The transfer-mirror rule assumes transfer rows are always symmetric: checking pays n, savings receives n. The correction path enforces that unconditionally, including rows whose stored postings deviate from the mirror — for example a transfer whose savings side was adjusted to include a fee or partial-transfer effect. Correcting such a row's amount silently rewrites the savings posting wholesale, discarding the deviation, and the application table shows only the checking-side change. The reviewer asked for one field; the answer rewrites two. Whether real ledgers ever carry asymmetric transfers is a data question; the code behavior is decided.

docs.title: An explicitly named file re applies even when already consumed if its content still parses
An explicitly named file re-applies even when already consumed, if its content still parses
Title
docs.text: An explicitly named file re-applies even when already consumed, if its content still parses

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The applied marker protects only the bulk sweep; feeding a consumed change-set by name to the single-file mode reads it again — re-applying JSON content, or crashing format-ugly on TOML files.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The rename-to-applied guarantee lives entirely in the sweep: nothing checks the marker at read time. When the single-file mode is pointed at an already-consumed file by its renamed name, the loader decides format purely by suffix and the consumed name's suffix matches neither of the two recognized ones — so it falls to the JSON reader. A formerly JSON change-set still parses as JSON and every fix in it applies a second time (corrections rebook the same content as fresh recorded changes). A formerly TOML change-set instead fails the JSON parse with a raw format error, telling the reviewer nothing about the file being spent. The same applies to a consumed file that was never renamed (crash window) — the file applies again. A reviewer expecting 'applied means inert' meets either silent double-application or a misleading error.

docs.title: Balance mismatch retries then cancels without storing a correction
Balance mismatch retries then cancels without storing a correction
Title
docs.text: Balance mismatch retries then cancels without storing a correction

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The projected-balance confirmation gives the bookkeeper three attempts to match the projected figure — and on the third mismatch the whole recording is cancelled instead of saving with the typed correction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When the interactive session shows the projected checking balance and the bookkeeper disagrees with it (they know the real position), they can retype the correct balance — but the code only accepts the confirmation when the typed figure matches the projection within half a cent. A deliberate correction — "I know the balance is really X" — is treated as a failed attempt: warned "does not match", and after three attempts the entire recording is thrown away. There is no path to save an entry with a balance override; the only surviving choice is to accept the projection or to record nothing.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Walking the whole edit form untouched on a still-future plan prints only the dim nothing-changed line and exits 0 — while the same all-Enter walk on a landed plan would have booked it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Two nearly identical sessions diverge by one date comparison. On a landed plan the untouched form books the plan (confirm intent); on a today-or-earlier check at edit.py:147 the branch is date-gated, and a future plan reaches the separate nothing-changed branch at edit.py:150-152, whose only output is '[dim]Niets gewijzigd.[/dim]' and a 0 exit. The bookkeeper gets no suggestion the landed case would have confirmed — the behavior gap is invisible until they try the same thing tomorrow. The code is deciding this consistently, so it is an oddity rather than an open question — but the asymmetry reads as unintended; the all-Enter confirm exists only where the date happens to have landed.

Title
docs.text: The bare delete picker shows only past rows

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: When the bookkeeper deletes without an id, the picker lists only the last ten rows dated today or earlier — future entries never appear to pick.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The bare delete command shows the committed view's last ten rows as a menu and asks which to delete. But the picker filters on date, not on kind — it takes rows whose date is not in the future. Committed entries are dated in the past or today, so the filter's real effect lands on anything unusual rather than on future-dated plan rows; plan rows carry plan-numbered ids the resolver would route to the expected register anyway. The oddity is the filter's bluntness — a date window standing where a kind check would read more naturally. The bookkeeper-visible effect is small — plan and rule rows are simply absent from the menu they pick from.

docs.title: The instance confirm id window hides landed instances older than the lookback
The instance-confirm id window hides landed instances older than the lookback
Title
docs.text: The instance-confirm id window hides landed instances older than the lookback

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A landed rule instance only resolves while it sits in the lookback-plus-grace window — an instance that stayed unconfirmed beyond that window can no longer be reached by id.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Confirming by instance id searches the active rules' projected instances inside a bounded window: from the ledger's anchor date minus a grace lookback, to today plus about thirteen months. An instance whose due date fell further in the past than that window — a bill nobody confirmed for weeks — is simply not found: the confirm call behaves as if the id were unknown. The same bounded reach applies to group members resolved through the instance path. The books themselves are the fallback (their covering superseding), but the direct one-step confirm of a long-ignored instance is not possible; the bookkeeper would book the payment the ordinary way instead.

# src/financials/recurrence_cli.py — lines 569–593
def _find_instance(entry_id: str) -> tuple[Recurrence, date] | None:
  """Resolve an r:-hash id to (rule, occurrence) among the ACTIVE rules'
  projected instances in [anchor − grace, +400d] — the same window as the
  view's open section, so landed-but-unconfirmed instances (including ones
  before an out-of-order-committed anchor) stay resolvable; no anchor
  falls back to the grace window from today. None = not a rule instance.
  Suppressed instances stay resolvable: expansion skips their dates, the
  dates themselves still exist."""
  from financials.ledger_view import _anchor_row, view_rows
  from financials.recurrences import _instances_for, instance_id

  today = TODAY()
  anchor = _anchor_row(view_rows(), today)
  window_start = (
    date.fromisoformat(anchor.date) - timedelta(days=RULE_LOOKBACK_DAYS)
    if anchor
    else today - timedelta(days=RULE_LOOKBACK_DAYS)
  )
  for rule in load_recurrences():
    if not rule.active:
      continue
    for occurrence in _instances_for(rule, window_start, today + timedelta(days=400)):
      if instance_id(rule, occurrence) == entry_id:
        return rule, occurrence
  return None

# src/financials/recurrences.py — lines 20–22
AMOUNT_TOLERANCE = 0.01
DAY_WINDOW = 5  # days around the rule day that a covering transaction may sit
RULE_LOOKBACK_DAYS = 35  # the view's grace lookback before the ledger's anchor

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Group confirmation re-points a member id using an expression whose branches collapse — if the re-pointing fires with no committed id, the original would silently become blank.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Inside the group confirm loop, the membership update for a confirmed plan member reassigns through a chained conditional built like "the new committed identifier, or the original — with the original spelled out on both halves of the branch". As written, the fallback that should keep the old id actually produces an empty string whenever the new id is absent, because the branch structure evaluates to the not-the-original arm regardless. Today the loop only re-points after _commit_expected returned a committed entry with an id, so the blank arm is unreachable in practice — but the expression will silently blank a member out of the group if that guard ever loosens. The safe form — new id when present, otherwise the original — is one nesting level off from what sits there.

Title
docs.text: The yearly proposal day rides the last occurrence of the pattern

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: For monthly and yearly proposals the day-of-month (and month) is taken from the most recent occurrence, not the first — so the proposal's anchor reflects the pattern's latest behaviour.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When the detector composes a proposal, the start field is the group's first occurrence (the phase anchor), but the day and month schedule fields come from the LAST occurrence in the sorted list. For a monthly pattern that drifted across month boundaries (e.g. paid the 31st, then the 30th, then the 1st), the proposed day is the most recent month's placement, and for yearly patterns likewise the latest month/day pair. The bookkeeper reviewing the table sees "Eerst" (first occurrence) next to a day-of-month derived from the end of the series — the proposal is internally consistent in cadence, but its day may not match its own first occurrence. Nothing wrong is stored (the approval loop shows the day as an editable default), but the displayed pair can puzzle at a glance.

docs.title: 1. Executive summary
docs.text:
It is a household ledger — the archetype story calls it a double-entry-adjacent personal ledger with a forecast layer — and its whole design protects one thing: books that can prove their own history.

  1. The books replay their own history: every change joins an append-only, content-hashed journal — timestamped so even identical same-day recordings stay distinct — and every row re-verifies on read; a correction is a new recorded event, never a quiet edit.
  2. Planned money cannot corrupt recorded money: recurring rules and their forecast are an overlay never materialized into the books, and the only bridge from plan to reality is the deliberately zero-prompt confirm of a landed entry.
  3. A caution for bulk-cleanup reviews: an amount correction on a transfer row silently overwrites any custom savings side — a reviewer fixing one field should expect both sides to rewrite.
  4. Destructive actions demand a typed affirmative and offer no undo; the journal — not a restore command — is the recovery story.

Verification status: no objection facts and no verification-phase records exist in the fact base at narration time, so these findings rest on the analyst passes' own confidence.

Next step: read the companion product summary and archetype mapping for the capability walk and concept map, then the per-surface detail sections.

docs.title: 2. Archetype mapping
docs.text:
The archetype is a double-entry-adjacent personal ledger with a forecast layer: a single-household bookkeeping suite that keeps an auditable account of committed money, a parking place for planned money, and a rules engine that turns history into forecast — nothing cloud-served, no multi-user world, just one household's two accounts kept provably true. Four core concepts carry the whole shape.

Actual versus expected is the load-bearing distinction: a movement either happened (dated today or earlier) and lives in the journaled books, or it is planned (dated ahead) and parks in a register that carries no balances. Nearly every rule and boundary in the project reads as a consequence of that one line.

Content-hash identity is the integrity archetype: a recording's identity is a hash of its own content plus creation time, appended to a journal that can never be edited — so the books replay their own history rather than remember it.

Running balances is the everyday payoff: every ledger row carries the balance it produced, so the household position at any date is a read, not a recalculation, and a backdated entry threads itself into the chain and pushes every later balance truthful again.

The approved category list is budgeting policy made executable — the household's own configured vocabulary is checked fresh at every recording on both the actual and the expected side.

Two further concepts organize the planner: a rule instance is a projected, virtual occurrence — real in the forecast, never in the books — and the confirmation backlog names what has landed but not yet been confirmed, one queue with one drain path.

How the concepts live in the components, in the component census's own order:

  • The transaction entry interface is where actual-versus-expected is policed at the front door — it validates, routes by date, and closes the loop with the projected-balance confirmation.
  • The confirmation dispatcher is the only bridge between the two worlds: it commits known values as recorded money without a conversation.
  • The interactive entry editor moves entries across that boundary by their corrected date — future edits turn recorded rows into plans, past-dated plans book into the ledger.
  • The recurrence engine is the forecast layer proper: rule store, projection of virtual instances, and the detection that proposes rules — never writing money itself.
  • The interactive deletion dispatcher is the four-way resolver: each store owns its own removal path, and destructive steps demand a typed affirmative.
  • The journaled ledger engine realizes content-hash identity and running balances — append, replay, verify, carry balances forward.
  • The expected register store is the planned-money world: strictly future-dated, balance-free, struck the moment a plan settles.
  • The cleanup fix engine treats corrections as reviewed, offline-authored change-set files (the change-set concept), each fix guarded — a fix may state the old value the ledger must confirm, the from-guard.

Basis note: this story rests on a deterministic sample of 12 of 17 concept facts, with all 17 censused; the 8 components were read in full.

docs.title: 3. Product summary
docs.text:
This is a household bookkeeping suite: typed commands over one household's checking and savings money, built so the books can always prove what was done to them. Everything rides one distinction — money that happened versus money that is only planned — and every capability below keeps that line sharp.

Recording a movement is the front door. The bookkeeper gives a spend or income as a one-line quick-add or through prompts that ask for anything missing; date, description, an approved category and a signed amount are checked — the category must be on the household's approved list — and the entry routes by its date: any future-dated entry parks in the expected register instead of the actual books, while moving money between the household's own accounts touches both balances at once. On the prompted path the balance is part of the deal: the projected checking balance is confirmed before anything saves, three mismatches throw the recording away, and no hand-corrected balance can ever be stored.

Confirming landed plans is the second door. When planned money arrives — a parked one-off entry, a due instance of a recurring rule, or a group of them — one confirm step commits the planned values with no questions asked, strikes the plan from the register, and answers an already-settled id harmlessly so nothing double-books. Adjusting values is deliberately the edit surface's job, done before confirming — never the confirm's.

Correcting walks one pre-filled form — Enter keeps a field, re-typing changes it, and only real changes are recorded. Where the correction lands follows the new date: a recorded entry corrected to today or earlier is journaled as a full restatement so later balances stay truthful; a recorded entry pushed into the future leaves the books and becomes a plan; a plan edited into the past books itself without further questions.

Recurring payments become standing rules. The tool scans the committed history for regularly repeating patterns, proposes them as read-only review rows — detection never creates a rule — and stores a rule only after the bookkeeper approves each detected field. An approved rule projects virtual due-dates into the forecast; it pauses, resumes, edits or retires without ever touching the books. The forecast is an overlay; only the bookkeeper's explicit confirmation of a due date creates recorded money.

Removing an entry is deliberate and loud. A typed id resolves in exactly one store — books, register, groups or rule occurrences — the row is shown, and a typed affirmative is required; bare Enter cancels. An actual transaction's removal is itself journal-recorded with its complete prior content, so history stays provable; the design offers no undo — re-creating a wrongly removed entry means recording it anew.

The books themselves are the spine: every business change joins an append-only journal as a mutation stamped with a creation time and a content hash, replayed into a ledger that carries each row's running balance and re-verifies every row on read. The household always sees the balance a recording produces, at any date, without recalculation.

Bulk corrections travel as reviewed change-set files: each fix names one known row, may state the old value it expects, and lands as exactly one recorded change; pending files sweep oldest first and are renamed applied when consumed. Cleanup can correct or trim history — it can never add rows to the actual books.

Where the product stops is design, not omission: balances are never hand-overridden at saving time, intake never asks for subcategories, confirmation never adjusts values, committed removals have no undo, and no automatic step ever writes recorded money on its own.

One honesty note on basis: the rule citations above rest on a deterministic sample of 12 of 60 business-rule facts, with all 60 censused; components, non-goals and processes were read in full.
