docs.title: No balance override at intake
docs.text: Statement: The intake deliberately offers no path to save a recording whose balance deviates from the projected books balance — the figure is confirmed or the recording is cancelled. Rationale: The confirmation gate's design: derived balances only. Whatever the bookkeeper types in the New checking-balance prompt, accepting is only possible within half a cent of the projection; deviating values are treated as failed confirmations, and three failures cancel. There is no "save anyway with my figure" branch, and no flag to bypass the gate. Whether an override door is wanted at all is a hotspot's question — but as built, the intake's answer is no.

docs.title: No subcategory prompt at intake
docs.text: Statement: The intake never asks for or stores a subcategory — new recordings carry empty subcategory fields even though the row shape and shorthand 'Category: description' form could host one. Rationale: The row shape carries a split-category (category plus optional subcategory kept from the retired importer), and the shorthand grammar's 'Head: tail' form could carry a subcategory — but intake assigns none. The prompt walks date, description, category, amount (and the balance confirmation) — no subcategory step exists, and the stored new entry's subcategory fields stay empty. Any subcategory discipline is a later stage's concern, not intake's.

docs.title: Confirmation never asks to adjust values
docs.text: Statement: The one-step confirm never prompts for date, description, category or amount of a landed plan; the interactive adjustments only exist on the separate future-instance path, not as an option of the landed confirm. Rationale: The confirm surface's own help text draws the boundary: confirm as-is, zero prompts, and "Adjust first: 'financials edit'". Even a landed plan's values arrive at the commit untouched — if the plan was wrong, the household workflow is to edit the plan, then confirm it. The only interactive confirm is the future-instance path (confirming an early-landed instance whose rule values need a real date/amount), which is a different business case, not a bypass of this boundary. The design keeps the fast path fast and puts all value corrections behind the edit door.

docs.title: Confirming writes no per-instance store
docs.text: Statement: Confirming a rule instance does not materialize or store the instance anywhere — only the ordinary booking exists after the commit, plus possibly an exception date on the rule. Rationale: The recurrence design keeps instances virtual: they are projected from rules for display, never stored as rows. Confirmation respects that boundary — the confirm books real money and never records "this instance was confirmed" except through the booking itself (and, when the booking drifted, an exception date on the rule so the stale projection leaves). There is deliberately no instance table, no confirmation log per instance, and no per-instance flag; the books' covering booking IS the confirmation record.

docs.title: The edit flow never edits rule instances or groups in place
docs.text: Statement: The edit resolver hands group ids and recurrence-instance ids to their own dedicated editors rather than correcting them through the transaction edit form. Rationale: When the id handed to edit resolves to a group or a rule instance, the resolver hands off — the group editor handles label, rollup date, category and note, and the occurrence editor handles the two-option rule-versus-exception choice. The transaction edit form (the four-field prompted pass) never edits these shapes in place. Deliberate boundary, not an omission: rule instances carry their own drift and exception rules, groups carry membership — both need different questions than the transaction form asks. The hand-off happens before the unknown-id refusal, so neither shape errors out of the edit surface.

docs.title: No undo for a committed removal
docs.text: Statement: The books deliberately offer no undo of a committed removal — the journal's audit trail is the only record of what was removed, and no command reverses it. Rationale: The delete module's docstring states the boundary plainly — there is no undo; the journal is the audit trail of what was removed. Re-creating a wrongly removed transaction means adding it again as a new entry, not restoring the old one. This is a deliberate design choice, not an oversight — the removal record with its full pre-image is the recoverability story. The household that wants an entry back re-enters it; the journal stays append-only in both directions.

docs.title: Recurring rules are never materialized into the transaction store
docs.text: Statement: The system deliberately never writes the recurring rules' projected instances into the actual books or any persistent instance store — instances exist only as the view-time projection, until a real booking supersedes or an explicit confirmation books one. Rationale: Two boundaries define the rule engine's honesty, both stated as owner decisions in the code's own words. The rule engine's module header: rules are never materialized into the transaction store — instance rows are computed fresh inside each view window and vanish with it. The command surface's header: the rule book is the recurring analogue of the expected register — overlay configuration, not journaled, because the journal is the story of committed money only. Together this means approving a rule, pausing it, or even the forecast showing a due bill never touches the books; only the bookkeeper's explicit confirmation of an instance creates journal entries, through the same doors as any booking. The forecast layer cannot corrupt the ledger by existing.

docs.title: A cleanup change-set never adds rows to the actual books
docs.text: Statement: The whole-row action set a cleanup file may use contains only removal of recorded rows, clearing of parked plans and parking of new planned entries — no action introduces a new row into the actual books. Rationale: A fix file can correct a row's fields or strike a row, and it can park a planned entry into the expected register (also a route for the interactive flows' internal ops list). It cannot create a new recorded transaction: no row-adding action exists in the change-set vocabulary, and the row engine refuses any action name outside its set. The boundary keeps cleanup files from becoming a second entry path — recorded history grows only at the entry interface, while cleanup only fixes or trims it.

docs.title: Balance mismatch retries then cancels without storing a correction (parity)
docs.text: Description: When the interactive session shows the projected checking balance and the bookkeeper disagrees with it (they know the real position), they can retype the correct balance — but the code only accepts the confirmation when the typed figure matches the projection within half a cent. A deliberate correction — "I know the balance is really X" — is treated as a failed attempt: warned "does not match", and after three attempts the entire recording is thrown away. There is no path to save an entry with a balance override; the only surviving choice is to accept the projection or to record nothing. Parity Relevance: None Impact: src/financials/entry.py:160-177

docs.title: First-entry date strictly after the last row is silently required (parity)
docs.text: Description: A recording whose date precedes every existing row cannot compute a balance base, and the code refuses it with a generic "no preceding row" message. On the interactive path the session shows the last row's date and a warning when that row is in the future (advising a later date) — but nothing guides the very first entry into an empty ledger: there, the refusal is bare, with no hint that "opening" rows are the intended fix. A bookkeeper landing here gets no suggestion that the opening position should be recorded first. Parity Relevance: None Impact: src/financials/entry.py:87-90, src/financials/entry.py:114-118

docs.title: The re-pointed member id wins over the original even on an unapplied commit (parity)
docs.text:
Description: Inside the group confirm loop, the membership update for a confirmed plan member reassigns through a chained conditional built like "the new committed identifier, or the original — with the original spelled out on both halves of the branch". As written, the fallback that should keep the old id actually produces an empty string whenever the new id is absent, because the branch structure evaluates to the not-the-original arm regardless. Today the loop only re-points after _commit_expected returned a committed entry with an id, so the blank arm is unreachable in practice — but the expression will silently blank a member out of the group if that guard ever loosens. The safe form — new id when present, otherwise the original — is one nesting level off from what sits there.

Parity Relevance: Any re-implementation of the group-confirm member re-point keeps the plain "new id if present, else old id" intent, not the odd branch spelling. Impact: src/financials/confirm.py:169

docs.title: A covered-instance skip inside group confirm checks only the checking posting (parity)
docs.text:
Description: Before committing a rule-instance member of a group, the code checks whether the books already hold a booking that covers the instance (same category, amount within a cent, date inside the window). That check, as spelled there, insists the covering booking carries a checking posting — and only the checking posting's amount is compared to the rule amount. The standalone view's own covering test compares the row's amount without that posting requirement. A rule projected on savings-side movements could therefore be re-committed by a group confirm even though a matching booking already exists on the savings side. In household practice every commit posts to checking, so the difference is latent, but the two covering tests are not the same rule as written.

Parity Relevance: Parity work must decide which covering test is canonical — the shared window/tolerance match, or the checking-posting-bound variant the group path spells — before copying either. Impact: src/financials/confirm.py:183-189, src/financials/recurrences.py:110-125

docs.title: The instance-confirm id window hides landed instances older than the lookback (exit-codes)
docs.text:
Description: Confirming by instance id searches the active rules' projected instances inside a bounded window: from the ledger's anchor date minus a grace lookback, to today plus about thirteen months. An instance whose due date fell further in the past than that window — a bill nobody confirmed for weeks — is simply not found: the confirm call behaves as if the id were unknown. The same bounded reach applies to group members resolved through the instance path. The books themselves are the fallback (their covering superseding), but the direct one-step confirm of a long-ignored instance is not possible; the bookkeeper would book the payment the ordinary way instead.

Parity Relevance: None Impact: src/financials/recurrence_cli.py:569-593, src/financials/recurrences.py:20-22

docs.title: Empty edit of an unlanded plan reports nothing changed with no follow-up (parity)
docs.text:
Description: Two nearly identical sessions diverge by one date comparison. On a landed plan the untouched form books the plan (confirm intent); on a today-or-earlier check at edit.py:147 the branch is date-gated, and a future plan reaches the separate nothing-changed branch at edit.py:150-152, whose only output is '[dim]Niets gewijzigd.[/dim]' and a 0 exit. The bookkeeper gets no suggestion the landed case would have confirmed — the behavior gap is invisible until they try the same thing tomorrow. The code is deciding this consistently, so it is an oddity rather than an open question — but the asymmetry reads as unintended; the all-Enter confirm exists only where the date happens to have landed.

Parity Relevance: None Impact: src/financials/edit.py:147-152

docs.title: Removing a transfer row warns about the savings chain (integrity)
docs.text: Description: A transfer row moves money between the checking and savings accounts — its removal therefore touches both account chains, not just checking. The command detects the transfer's category after the deletion succeeds and prints a yellow note that removing a transfer also affects the savings chain, advising the bookkeeper to review the ledger listing afterwards. This is a heads-up, not a gate — the deletion has already been applied when the warning is shown, and no follow-up action is forced. Parity Relevance: None Impact: src/financials/delete.py:69-73

docs.title: The bare delete picker shows only past rows (parity)
docs.text: Description: The bare delete command shows the committed view's last ten rows as a menu and asks which to delete. But the picker filters on date, not on kind — it takes rows whose date is not in the future. Committed entries are dated in the past or today, so the filter's real effect lands on anything unusual rather than on future-dated plan rows; plan rows carry plan-numbered ids the resolver would route to the expected register anyway. The oddity is the filter's bluntness — a date window standing where a kind check would read more naturally. The bookkeeper-visible effect is small — plan and rule rows are simply absent from the menu they pick from. Parity Relevance: None Impact: src/financials/delete.py:77-92

docs.title: A rule that already exists is appended again on every approval (parity)
docs.text: Description: The detector's dedup rule (never re-propose a covered pattern) is the only dedup the flow has. The hand-add path, proposal adoption and even the edit path simply append the (possibly edited) rule object to the loaded list and save — no uniqueness check on description plus category anywhere on the write side. The bookkeeper can therefore store two rules with identical pattern fields by adding twice or by editing a rule's description into another rule's description; both will project their instances into every future period, doubling the forecast. The superseding matcher softens the visual symptom slightly (a covering booking retires one instance of each), but two identical rules stay on the books as two. The collision refusal lives only in the vault, so to speak — not in the store. Parity Relevance: A parity port must decide whether uniqueness is checked at write time or trusted to the detector's read-time exclusion; the current code trusts it. Impact: src/financials/recurrence_cli.py:464-466, src/financials/recurrence_cli.py:946-948, src/financials/recurrence_cli.py:561-562

docs.title: The yearly proposal day rides the last occurrence of the pattern (parity)
docs.text:
Description: When the detector composes a proposal, the start field is the group's first occurrence (the phase anchor), but the day and month schedule fields come from the LAST occurrence in the sorted list. For a monthly pattern that drifted across month boundaries (e.g. paid the 31st, then the 30th, then the 1st), the proposed day is the most recent month's placement, and for yearly patterns likewise the latest month/day pair. The bookkeeper reviewing the table sees "Eerst" (first occurrence) next to a day-of-month derived from the end of the series — the proposal is internally consistent in cadence, but its day may not match its own first occurrence. Nothing wrong is stored (the approval loop shows the day as an editable default), but the displayed pair can puzzle at a glance. Parity Relevance: None Impact: src/financials/recurrences.py:293-300

docs.text: Term Description expected / actual plan versus the real recorded movement (the household's "expected" entries versus the factual rows in the actual books) Overdracht moving money between the household's own accounts — the category whose postings touch both checking and savings Bevestigd: {t.id} → {entry.id} The landed plan is confirmed — it became a booking and left the register. entry, _ = ledger.find(entry_id); find_entry(entry_id, [], load_expected()) resolving the bookkeeper's chosen entry — the row they picked from the list to correct Tier A / Tier B Same-amount patterns versus timely-but-varying patterns Kandidaat-regels Candidate rules (the detector's proposal table) fix file keys: id, field, from, to, op, reason; op values remove_row, add_expected_row; files cleanup_fixes(.json|.toml) renamed to .applied A cleanup change-set: each fix names a row (id), what to change (field, the old value from, the new value to) or which whole-row action to take (op), and why (reason); a consumed file is marked applied.

docs.title: Date comparison as ISO strings
docs.text: Every future/past dispatch decision in the intake compares ISO date strings lexically, not calendar dates — any non-padded or malformed date string can flip the routing decision, and only the later date-format validation catches the malformed cases. Found in: src/financials/entry.py:220, src/financials/entry.py:126-128, src/financials/entry.py:73-75, src/financials/expected.py:66-69

docs.title: Balance projection must agree with the engine's chaining
docs.text: The interactive confirmation shows a projected checking balance derived from the ledger's date-positioned predecessor, and it must be computed with the same logic the engine will apply on saving — any divergence shows the bookkeeper a figure the engine will not produce. Found in: src/financials/entry.py:154-158, src/financials/commands.py:179-192

docs.title: The register strike must never precede a successful commit
docs.text: The delete of the plan row happens only after the confirming booking has applied and returned a committed row; striking first would destroy a plan whose payment never got recorded. Found in: src/financials/confirm.py:39-43, src/financials/confirm.py:46-47, src/financials/confirm.py:57-61

docs.title: Instance resolution depends on the ledger's anchor row
docs.text: Which rule instances confirm can see depends on where the ledger's anchor date currently sits — a long-unconfirmed ledger shifts the reachable window, and the confirm paths inherit that sensitivity. Found in: src/financials/recurrence_cli.py:569-593, src/financials/recurrences.py:20-22

docs.title: The move-to-expected hole can leave an entry in neither store
docs.text: The move path deletes the committed entry before creating the planned replacement, so a rejection at the second step destroys the entry with no automatic undo — only a manual rebuild via the expect command. Found in: src/financials/edit.py:213-229

docs.title: Transfer edits and moves must keep the savings mirror truthful
docs.text: Any edit or move of a transfer (Overdracht) touches two account chains — the checking posting and the mirrored savings posting — and the planned register holds only the checking shape, so moves need an explicit savings-side check. Found in: src/financials/commands.py:88-95, src/financials/edit.py:231-235, src/financials/edit.py:266-270

docs.title: Rule suppression matches by description and category
docs.text: The suppression writes the exception onto every rule whose description and category both match the scanned instance — a same-worded pair of rules would take the exception together. Found in: src/financials/recurrence_cli.py:839-843

docs.title: Stale-pre-image refusal halts the entire boot
docs.text: A mismatching removal record does not only block its own deletion — the value error rises through the replay and the books refuse to open at all. Found in: src/financials/journal.py:323-346, src/financials/journal.py:526-532, src/financials/journal.py:516-520

docs.title: Proposal numbering resolves only against a fresh detector run
docs.text: Adopting a proposal by number recomputes the proposal table at adoption time — the number is only meaningful when history and existing rules have not changed since the table was shown. Found in: src/financials/recurrence_cli.py:914-927, src/financials/recurrence_cli.py:860-862

docs.title: Whole-file rule overwrite keeps every writer honest about reload-then-save
docs.text:
Every rule mutation reloads the store from disk immediately before rewriting it — a writer that edited an in-memory list from an earlier read would silently erase changes another command made in between. Found in: src/financials/recurrences.py:49-54, src/financials/recurrence_cli.py:464-466, src/financials/recurrence_cli.py:528

docs.title: 1. Issues
docs.text:
Note

While analyzing the codebase, our agents often encounter issues. Although not strictly part of the analysis, we report them because they often hold valuable information where the current implementation fails.

We identify four kinds:

  • code-bug: the implementation has a mistake that hinders the intended functionality
  • docs-drift: the documentation does not match the implementation and the documents are the stale side
  • docs-code-conflict: the mismatch is demonstrated but neither side is attributable yet
  • functional-mistake: the implemented behavior contradicts the established functional facts with no documented claim involved

docs.title: Financials add help offers a checking-balance flag the intake ignores
docs.text:
Classification: docs-code-conflict

Summary: The command's own help advertises "New checking balance (defaults to the continued balance)" for --checking, but the value is passed through and never used — a recording can never carry a hand-stated balance.

Claim: New checking balance (defaults to the continued balance).

Rationale: Read the dispatcher's add wiring (cli.py main, add branch) and the intake call chain (add_transaction entry.py:181-287). The claim comes from the add parser's own --checking help text (cli.py:80-85). Tracing the flag's value: args.checking is forwarded to add_transaction(checking=...) at cli.py:283; a syntactic reference search of entry.py shows checking appears only in _prompt internals (108, 112, 167, 171, 172) and the unused parameter declaration (186) — the parameter's value is never read anywhere in the function body. So a caller-supplied balance cannot influence any stored balance, contradicting the advertised "new checking balance" behavior. Neither side is trivially the stale one — the derived-only balance design at the confirmation gate (entry.py:160-177) may be what stranded the flag; both the help and the code stand coherent internally, so the conflict is parked for review rather than attributed.

docs.title: Financials add help undersells the shorthand grammar
docs.text:
Classification: docs-code-conflict

Summary: The command's help claims the quick-add slot order "[date] [amount] [Category:]description", but the parser also accepts relative day words and dates/amounts only in that fixed first-two slots — wordier than advertised, yet stricter elsewhere.

Claim: Quick-add: "[date] [amount] [Category:]description" (date: ISO / vandaag / gisteren / morgen / -3d).

Rationale: Compared the dispatcher's shorthand help (cli.py:91-98) against the traced parser (shorthand.py:101-138). The grammar promise "[Category:]description" is right about slot ordering and the day words. The gap: the parser only promotes the colon-headed part to the category when it canonicalizes against the approved list (shorthand.py:132-137); otherwise the whole remaining text is description. The help never states that the head must be an approved category — a bookkeeper typing "Winkel: brood" gets category=None and is prompted, reading the help as a contract. Neither side is plainly stale: the parser's behavior is deliberate (conservative resolution, docstring states it), and the help condenses it wrongly. Parked as a conflict for review.

docs.title: Bare confirm help text omits group ids the command actually accepts
docs.text:
Classification: docs-code-conflict

Summary: The confirm command's help promises plan ids and rule instance ids, but the dispatch also confirms group ids with their own path — the help text and the accepted id families diverge.

Claim: "Confirm an open entry in one go: a landed expected entry (e####) or rule instance (r:...) commits as-is, zero prompts. Adjust first: 'financials edit'. Bare confirm shows the OPEN section."

Rationale: Read the confirm parser definition (cli.py:140-153): the id argument's help names only expected entries and rule instances. Read the dispatch (confirm_transaction, confirm.py:232-261): the first branch tests the group family and routes to the group walk, which is real confirmed behavior (I traced the group walk in confirm.py:124-202 this engagement). Consulted: the surface command fact (financials-confirm), the group confirmation rule, and the group entity. The claim is verbatim from the help string; the code demonstrably accepts a third id family the claim never mentions — a demonstrated mismatch; attribution (help drift vs intentionally hidden feature) is not decidable from the code.

docs.title: Group confirm covered-skip note claims a booked row settled the member even when the member is a plan
docs.text:
Classification: functional-mistake

Summary: The covered-instance skip note is worded as if a booked row already settled the member; in the group loop the same covered logic also applies to rule-instance members only — but its dim wording suggests settledness the view may not show.

Claim: {member_id} is al gedekt door een geboekte rij — overgeslagen.

Rationale: Consulted the group confirm loop's covered test (confirm.py:183-189) against the projection's covering test (recurrences.py:110-125): the confirm path requires a checking posting and compares the posting amount; the projection's test compares amount_eur with no posting requirement and year-matches the date prefix. The skip message (string-literal, confirm.py:191) asserts settledness in the projection's vocabulary while the group path uses a different test. No docstring or help claims the two tests agree, so this is a functional discrepancy between two implementations, not a documented-claim conflict; per the family's boundary law it is recorded with the vocabulary-only class and stays out of my emission set as a side-class — flagged for review instead.

docs.title: Edit help omits that bare edit also reaches plans, groups and rule instances
docs.text:
Classification: docs-code-conflict

Summary: The command help says the id argument picks from the last ten actual rows when omitted — and the resolver does that — but the help never mentions the future-plan register, group-editor or occurrence-editor branches the bare path and unusual ids reach.

Claim: Id from 'financials list' (omit to pick from the last 10 actual rows).

Rationale: Consulted the argparse help text at cli.py:113-123 (the claim verbatim at :122), the edit resolver at edit.py:274-319, and the picker at edit.py:123-138. The help states the two documented paths verbatim; the resolver demonstrably accepts e#### (routes to _edit_expected at :304), g#### (edit.py:288-293) and r:… ids (edit.py:298-301), and the bare path filters rows to today-or-earlier before slicing the last ten (:127-128) — so the bare list truly holds only actual rows, matching the help's wording, but the id side of the help never mentions the plan, group or instance surfaces. Neither side is attributable — the help is not wrong about what it says, the resolver is not wrong about what it does; classified docs-code-conflict and left for review.

docs.title: Module docstring promises unambiguous-prefix id resolution the resolver never performs
docs.text:
Classification: docs-code-conflict

Summary: The delete module claims full and prefix id matching on committed rows; the actual ledger lookup is exact-match only, so a prefix quietly reports "Onbekende id".

Claim: Resolves the id in the committed ledger (hash id, full or unambiguous prefix) or the expected register (e####), shows the row, and requires an explicit confirmation (bare Enter is NOT yes).

Rationale: Consulted the module docstring as the claim, the ledger's own lookup (journal.py find, 177-185) which enumerates and compares each stored row's id for exact equality with no prefix handling anywhere on the delete path, the delete dispatcher (delete.py:105-143) which passes the typed id straight into that lookup, and the group resolver (groups.py:82-102) which alone implements prefix and name matching — for groups only. No prefix matcher for ledger rows was found on the traced path, and query_references shows no 'startswith' under delete.py at all. The claim's falsity is demonstrated on the code side; which side is wrong (stale docstring describing an older behaviour, or a promised feature never wired) cannot be decided from code alone, so the conflict stays unattributed.

docs.title: Recurrence add help names only monthly and yearly while add accepts all four cadences
docs.text:
Classification: docs-code-conflict

Summary: The command parser's own help for the frequency flag undersells the surface — weekly and biweekly rules (with their weekday anchor) work, including through the seeded editor, but the help says "monthly | yearly (add)".

Claim: monthly | yearly (add)

Rationale: Consulted the --frequency help string at the parser (cli.py:248) as the claim; against it, the validation gate (recurrence_cli.py:160-161) which enumerates monthly|yearly|weekly|biweekly as the accepted values on the very same add path, the add function's weekday handling (recurrence_cli.py:400-410) which asks and snaps anchors for weekly/biweekly, the module's dataclass comment (recurrences.py:30) listing all four frequencies, and list/confirm outputs renderingweekly and biweekly. Weekly and biweekly demonstrably work on the add path, so the help omits supported values. Which side is wrong — stale help or an intended flag-time restriction the code forgot to enforce — is not decidable from the code; left unattributed for review.

docs.title: The retry limit constant sits defined but unread in the recurrence module
docs.text:
Classification: functional-mistake

Summary: The recurrence command module defines a retry limit constant that nothing in the module reads — the three-retries discipline lives in other modules' own copies, and this one is dead weight on the rule surface.

Claim: RETRY_LIMIT = 3

Rationale: Consulted the constant definition at recurrence_cli.py:42 and the name trace across the codebase: every use of RETRY_LIMIT sits in entry.py, edit.py and ask.py, which define their own copies for their prompt-retry loops; the recurrence module's identifier appears exactly once — the defining line itself (query_references and query_callers agree, zero in-module reads). Dead on this surface, but no documented behaviour claim is involved, so recorded as a functional note rather than a claim-based divergence; the review phase may prefer deleting the line.

docs.title: Design doc names a balance-rebase helper in the fix engine that the code no longer has
docs.text:
Classification: docs-code-conflict

Summary: The ledger design log's step-6 section names rebase-checking-side logic as living in the fix engine file, but no such function exists anywhere in the codebase.

Claim: rebase_checking (fixes.py) already implements the replay rule

Rationale: Consulted: the design log step-6 section around the claim (docs/journaled-ledger.md, retrieval filtered on rebase/fixes), the fix engine's full symbol inventory (outline listing 11 symbols, file lines 61-274) — no symbol resembling a balance-rebase helper exists there — and a repo-wide name search returning zero occurrences. The claim is a specific, verifiable existence assertion; its failure is demonstrated. Attribution fails both ways: the doc carries dated design-decision marks but no explicit removal note for this helper, and the current update-as-rebook design (rule fact: a committed correction rebooks the row) makes the helper plausibly obsolete rather than missing-by-mistake. Classification therefore stays at the demonstrated state: the mismatch is real, neither side provably stale or buggy.

docs.title: 2. Hotspots
docs.text:
Note

Sometimes our agents encounter a bump in the road, an implementation that is so obscure or a comment that is so incomprehensible, that they need your ruling to make sense out of it.

These situations are reported as hotspots because they probably cover a dark secret that, when resolved, not only improved the analysis, but might also help to improve the implementation if needed.

In contrast to issues, hotspots deal with functional uncertainty, yet the answer to their questions might result in a new issue.

docs.title: Whether a balance correction override is wanted
docs.text:
Summary: The confirmation loop can only confirm or cancel; there is no saving path when the bookkeeper disagrees with the projection. Whether that is intended policy or a missing feature is a business decision the code cannot answer.

Description: When a spend was actually made from a cash stash or an unlisted account, the real checking balance after it differs from what the books will project. The intake's confirmation loop offers exactly two endings: accept the projected figure, or have the recording cancelled after three attempts — a deliberate "the balance is really X" cannot be recorded. There is no policy text in the code or docs stating whether the household wants balances strictly derived (derived-only) or an override door for reconciliation. The behavior is coherent and the code decides it; the intent behind it is business-decided.

Question: Should the household ever be able to save a recorded movement whose balance they know to differ from the projected books balance — a deliberate balance correction — or is refusing to record-on-mismatch the intended policy?

docs.title: Whether the checking-only preview is the intended projection
docs.text:
Summary: The confirmation gate projects and confirms only the checking side, while a transfer recording also moves savings; whether the confirmation should mirror that is a business question, not decidable from code.

Description: The intake's confirmation loop works the checking account only: the projection shown, typed and matched is checking-only. The posting rule, however, moves two accounts for a transfer (checking in, savings out — mirror). A bookkeeper confirming a transfer's checking projection is never asked about the savings side. The code offers no evidence of the intended policy: is savings implicitly trusted to follow the mirror, or is its omission at the gate a gap? The behavior is observable; the intent is not.

Question: Should the pre-save projection confirm the checking balance only, or should it also account for savings — e.g. when the recording is a transfer the household considers as touching both accounts?

docs.title: Whether the parked --checking flag should be fixed or retired
docs.text:
Summary: The advertised flag does nothing; whether the intended fix is an override path or a removal of the promise is a product decision the code cannot answer.

Description: The dispatcher passes --checking into the intake and the intake ignores it; the help text still promises a "new checking balance". Two coherent readings exist: the flag is a leftover from a pre-derived-balances design and should disappear (aligning with the derived-only confirmation gate), or the balance-override door should be finished (aligning with the help). The code shows the current state but not which direction the household wants — a business call, made with the balance-override hotspot.

Question: Should the --checking flag on financials add actually set the recording's starting balance, or should the unused flag (and its help promise) be removed so the surface no longer advertises a balance override the intake refuses?

docs.title: Group confirm exit codes report partial success as full success
docs.text:
Summary: A group confirm that confirms some members and skips others exits 0; only a group with nothing landable exits nonzero — the code's choice, not the business's, is unrecorded anywhere.

Description: When a group is confirmed, future-dated, amountless, unresolvable and already-covered members are each skipped with a on-screen note, while landable members commit; the command then exits as a success. Only the case where nothing at all could be confirmed exits nonzero. The code makes this choice consistently, but nothing in the help text or documentation states that "some members skipped" counts as success — whether that is the intended business signal (e.g. because the notes are enough for a human) or an unconsidered default is not decidable from the code. The answer lives with the business, not the analysis.

Question: Should the confirm command report a partially-confirmed group as success (today's behavior — exit 0 with skip notes), or should the skipped members surface as a distinct failure-like signal so pipelines and scripts can react?

docs.title: The interactive instance confirm books real values the rule no longer knows
docs.text:
Summary: The interactive path lets the bookkeeper shift the date and amount of an instance's confirm; the code then records an exception so the projection does not linger — but whether the rule's standing pattern should absorb the change is nowhere answered.

Description: The interactive instance confirm exists so an early-landed bill (or one with a different real amount) can be confirmed with its real values. The commit then finds the values no longer cover the rule's period and records the occurrence date as an exception. That keeps the view honest, but it means the standing rule drifts from reality: the following month the rule again projects the old pattern day and old amount, while the household has now paid differently once. Whether the business wants the rule edited (so future instances adopt the new reality) or accepts a one-off exception (the bill was just odd) cannot be determined from the code — the code only implements the exception path. The answer lives with the business, not the analysis.

Question: When the interactive confirm of a rule instance changes date or amount so the booking drifts outside the rule's covering window, should the rule itself be adjusted (its pattern day or amount updated to match reality), or is only the one-off exception date the intended outcome?

docs.title: Should the failed move rebuild or refund the deleted actual row
docs.text:
Summary: The delete-first sequencing leaves a bookkeeper-visible hole — whether an automatic undo belongs there is a business decision, not decidable from the code.

Description: The move route removes the committed row first (edit.py:214) and creates the planned entry second (edit.py:218). When the second step rejects, the row exists nowhere — the code prints the recovery hint naming the expect command and stops. The deletion is a journaled mutation, so a rebuild would be a new mutation sequence (a re-add), possible to compose — the question is whether the business wants silent self-healing of a failed move, or prefers the current explicit human recovery. The answer lives with the business, not the analysis — the code alone cannot say whether that behavior is intended or just the current sequencing.

Question: When the move-to-expected deletes a committed row and the planned replacement then fails to save, should the code automatically rebuild the original actual row instead of leaving recovery to the bookkeeper?

docs.title: The expected register has two removal doors with different safety
docs.text:
Summary: The delete command always asks before removing a planned entry; the standalone expected-entry removal never asks, and the code shows no evidence of which behaviour is intended.

Description: There are two paths to strike a planned entry: the delete command (row printed, typed confirmation required) and the standalone expect-removal surface (silently removes by id, no prompt whatsoever — the only removal path in the codebase with no confirmation). Which is deliberate and which is an oversight is not decidable from the code: the standalone path's docstring and help text both claim a plain remove without warning, so the claim is at least self-consistent there; yet the household's other removal surfaces all enforce the confirm-first law, and a typo'd id removes a plan in one keystroke on this path. The business must decide which policy owns planned-entry removal.

Question: Should a planned entry be removable without an explicit typed confirmation through the expect-removal surface, when the delete command's whole design says every removal asks first?

docs.title: The bare delete picker's date filter reaches rows beyond its purpose
docs.text:
Summary: The picker filters menu rows by date rather than by kind — its effect on today's or past-dated non-committed rows is not decidable from the code.

Description: The bare delete command shows a pick menu built from the ledger view's rows, keeping only rows whose date is not in the future. The intent the docstring names is a menu of past actual rows, and on today's data committed rows are past-dated, so the behaviour looks right — but the filter reaches anything with an old date, whatever its kind, and the ledger view's row list is the composed view, not the raw committed list. Whether a kind check was intended, or the date window is deliberate (perhaps to let transfers dated today appear), is a design question the code cannot answer — the business owns which reading is meant.

Question: Should the bare delete picker only ever offer committed past rows (a kind check) rather than filtering by date, which reaches any row dated today or earlier?

docs.title: Whether the two-month gap should classify a monthly pattern
docs.text:
Summary: The gap bands make a skipped month (gap ~60 days) fail every band, so a seasonal-but-mostly-monthly bill is never proposed; whether that is the intended strictness is a business call.

Description: The classifier accepts a cadence only when enough consecutive gaps fall inside its band; a monthly band spans 26–38 days, so a single skipped month produces a gap of about 60 days that matches nothing. The weekly band has an explicit tolerance for one skipped week (the band overlaps biweekly's), but the monthly band has no such slack — one missed month kills an otherwise long monthly streak for proposal purposes. The code shows what the threshold currently does; whether the business wants a mostly-monthly but occasionally-skipped bill (someone on holiday, a waived fee) to surface as a proposal is not decidable from the code. The answer lives with the household's owner, not the analysis.

Question: Should a repeating payment that skips one month entirely — a gap of roughly sixty days inside an otherwise monthly streak — still be recognized and proposed as a monthly rule, or is silence the intended behaviour for months the pattern did not appear?

docs.title: Sweep order sorts file names, not review sequence
docs.text:
Summary: The pending sweep orders files by name; whether that reliably equals review order depends on the bookkeeper's file-naming convention, which the tool does not enforce.

Description: The sweep sorts pending cleanup files by their names and applies the first name first, presenting this as oldest-first. The intent is that corrections reach the ledger in the same order the reviewer produced and reviewed them. But nothing in the code ties a file's name to when it was authored: the oldest-first claim holds only if the bookkeeper names files so that name order encodes time (dates in names). No surface communicates or validates that convention. Whether names-in-date-format is an assumption the business is willing to live with — versus a stated naming convention the tool should check — is a question for the people running the process.

Question: Should the sweep's oldest-first order follow the file names' alphabetical order, or should it follow the order in which the reviews happened when names share a timestamp convention that alphabetical order does not reflect?

docs.title: Reviewer remarks never reach the permanent record
docs.text:
Summary: Fix files carry a free-text reason per fix, shown only while the change-set runs; nothing stores it beyond that print and the applied file's content on disk.

Description: The cleanup tables printed during application show each fix's stated reason beside each change. The reviewer wrote those reasons as part of the reviewed file. They are not recorded anywhere in the system's own stores: the change journal carries only the corrected row states (never the reasons), and nothing else persists them. The only surviving trace is the applied file itself sitting renamed on disk. Whether that is the intended division — the file is the review record and the system's journal is the execution record — or the reasons ought to ride into the permanent record for auditors, is a business decision the code cannot make.

Question: Should the reason text a reviewer attaches to each fix be preserved in the permanent record, or is the change journal alone the intended audit trail of record?

def postings_for(category: str, amount: float) -> dict[str, float]:
  """The posting set for an amount in a category: checking carries the
  amount; a transfer carries the savings mirror (the engine moves both
  balances)."""
  postings = {"checking": round(amount, 2)}
  if category == "Overdracht":
    postings["savings"] = round(-amount, 2)
  return postings

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The detector's two proposal tiers map to two real household shapes — a bill paid the same amount each period, and a bill confirmed at its actual (varying) spend each period.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The code's tier names are workflow vocabulary in disguise. Tier A — the original constant-amount detector — is the household's fixed bill: rent, subscription, salary; every occurrence within roughly five percent of the median. Tier B is the household's budget-style pattern: the same recurring payment confirmed each period with the actual spend, timely but variable — proposed at the median with the observed range attached, and refusing groups that move money both directions. When Tier A's dates fail to classify, Tier B gets a second look over all occurrences; the tiers are the code's names for these two shapes of household life.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: When a removal fix misses the actual books, the tool consults the expected register before refusing — clearing the parked plan takes precedence over the unknown-target abort.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The whole-row removal path first resolves the fix's designation in the committed ledger. If it finds nothing, two rules want to govern: the removal engine's unknown-target refusal (abort the fix loudly, nothing happens) and the register-clearing rule (the designation may name a parked entry, which the fix removes). The traced branching decides it: the engine asks the expected register next, and a match there removes the plan and reports the change — the refusal never fires. The refusal remains the governing rule only when the register also holds no match. Consequence for the business: one reviewed file can clean up both book rows and parked plans, but the ordering is invisible unless a reviewer knows the register is consulted as a fallback.

docs.text: The plan disappears from the register and the run reports the plan removal, where a books-only reviewer would have expected the unknown-target abort.

docs.title: For a drifted instance commit the explicit exception beats the silent superseding
For a drifted instance commit the explicit exception beats the silent superseding
Title
docs.text: For a drifted instance commit the explicit exception beats the silent superseding

docs.title: Condition
docs.text: The bookkeeper confirms a due rule instance with values that changed — an amount beyond a cent's tolerance or a date moved beyond the window around the rule day — so the new booking no longer still counts as covering the instance's period.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: When the confirming booking still covers the rule's period, the instance simply disappears (superseded); when it drifted, the confirmation additionally writes the occurrence as an exception on the rule — the explicit retirement rule governs the drifted case so the instance cannot linger.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Two rules meet at this branch. The silent superseding rule says an instance leaves the open view as soon as a real booking covers its period — nothing to record. The drift rule says a confirming booking that no longer matches (amount beyond tolerance, date outside the window) must be recorded as an exception on the recurrence rule, because the covering test would fail and the projection would keep showing the instance as due forever. The commit core makes the precedence explicit: it performs the matching test on the values actually committed, and only when that test fails does it write the exception date. So the covering rule governs the unchanged case (no exception written — writing one there would be harmless but wasteful) and the exception rule governs the drifted case, where without it the ghost instance would survive its own confirmation.

docs.title: Visible Effect
docs.text: The drifted confirmation commits the real payment with the changed values, and the projected instance leaves the open view; the rule carries the occurrence date as an exempt instance from then on.

def _covers(occurrence: date, rule: Recurrence, transactions: list[Transaction]) -> bool:
  """True when a real transaction covers this rule instance's period."""
  window_lo = occurrence - timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  window_hi = occurrence + timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  for t in transactions:
    if not t.date or not t.date.startswith(str(occurrence.year)):
      continue
    t_date = date.fromisoformat(t.date)
    if not (window_lo <= t_date <= window_hi):
      continue
    if t.category != rule.category:
      continue
    if t.amount_eur is None or abs(t.amount_eur - rule.amount) > AMOUNT_TOLERANCE:
      continue
    return True
  return False

Title
docs.text: On a committed entry a future-dated edit move beats the journaled full replacement

docs.title: Condition
docs.text: A recorded entry is edited and the edited date falls after today.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The move rule wins — the entry leaves the ledger as a planned entry instead of receiving a journaled update, when the edited date is future.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Two rules both claim a committed-entry edit. The journaled-replacement rule says the correction appends an update mutation. The future-date move rule says a committed row edited to a future date must leave the ledger and reappear as a planned entry. The branching resolves it: the editor checks the edited date against today first (edit.py:251) and routes to the move path; only a date of today or earlier reaches the journaled update. A future-dated recorded entry is not something the ledger can hold, so the move rule governs exactly where both claims meet.

docs.title: Visible Effect
docs.text: The recorded row is removed from the ledger and re-created as a planned entry at the future date — no update mutation is journaled for that case.

def _covers(occurrence: date, rule: Recurrence, transactions: list[Transaction]) -> bool:
  """True when a real transaction covers this rule instance's period."""
  window_lo = occurrence - timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  window_hi = occurrence + timedelta(days=DAY_WINDOW)
  for t in transactions:
    if not t.date or not t.date.startswith(str(occurrence.year)):
      continue
    t_date = date.fromisoformat(t.date)
    if not (window_lo <= t_date <= window_hi):
      continue
    if t.category != rule.category:
      continue
    if t.amount_eur is None or abs(t.amount_eur - rule.amount) > AMOUNT_TOLERANCE:
      continue
    return True
  return False

Title

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: A change-set that fails partway through its fixes leaves every earlier fix in the file applied — nothing rolls back — so the reviewer must know that a re-run re-applies only the remainder.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Application is per-fix, not per-file: the applied prefix stays, the failed file stays pending, and a repaired re-run continues rather than duplicating.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When a fix in a change-set fails its guards (unknown row, stale old value, ambiguous prefix), the exception aborts at that fix: the fixes before it in the same file are already recorded as separate, complete ledger changes. The file is not renamed, so the next sweep or file-mode run retries the file from the top — and the earlier fixes will then either fail their now-mismatched from-guards or apply their corrections a second time, depending on how the reviewer repairs the file. The engine takes no snapshot and offers no bulk undo; recovery is the reviewer's decision, guided by the ledger's own record of what the first pass actually changed.

def projected_checking(

  (projection, predecessor); (None, None) when no predecessor exists."""

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Confirming a rule instance by id does not search all history: it searches from the ledger's anchor date minus a lookback, to today plus about thirteen months. def _find_instance(entry_id: str) -> tuple[Recurrence, date] | None:
  """Resolve an r:-hash id to (rule, occurrence) among the ACTIVE rules'
  projected instances in [anchor − grace, +400d] — the same window as the
  view's open section, so landed-but-unconfirmed instances (including ones
  before an out-of-order-committed anchor) stay resolvable; no anchor
  falls back to the grace window from today. None = not a rule instance.
  Suppressed instances stay resolvable: expansion skips their dates, the
  dates themselves still exist."""
  from financials.ledger_view import _anchor_row, view_rows
  from financials.recurrences import _instances_for, instance_id

  today = TODAY()
  anchor = _anchor_row(view_rows(), today)
  window_start = (
    date.fromisoformat(anchor.date) - timedelta(days=RULE_LOOKBACK_DAYS)
    if anchor
    else today - timedelta(days=RULE_LOOKBACK_DAYS)
  )
  for rule in load_recurrences():
    if not rule.active:
      continue
    for occurrence in _instances_for(rule, window_start, today + timedelta(days=400)):
      if instance_id(rule, occurrence) == entry_id:
        return rule, occurrence
  return None

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: A consumed file is renamed only after its full application succeeds; a crash or refusal at any fix leaves the file pending, so the applied marker must never be trusted as complete by itself.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The sweep applies each pending file's fixes and only then renames the file. Between the final fix's journal line and the rename there is a window: a crash there leaves the file pending while all its fixes are applied. On the next run the file applies again — each fix re-resolves against the ledger; corrections rebook the same content (a no-op rebook), unguarded field fixes reapply harmlessly to the identical row, guard-protected fixes refuse with a stale-value message naming the already-corrected value. The outcome converges to the right books but the reviewer sees refusals that look like failures. Interpreting those messages correctly — as an applied-twice marker rather than a broken file — needs process knowledge no surface teaches.

docs.text: The suppression writes the exception onto every rule whose description and category both match the scanned instance — a same-worded pair of rules would take the exception together.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The match is value-based, not identity-based — two rules wearing the same description and category are indistinguishable to suppression.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: After the bookkeeper confirms a suppression, the code scans the reloaded rule list and marks every rule with the scanned instance's description and category, adding the occurrence date to each match's exceptions. There is no rule id in the match — a household that somehow holds two rules with identical wording and category would have the same occurrence suppressed on both. For a single bookkeeper's rules this is unlikely, but the match's width is worth knowing before editing rule data by hand.

docs.title: Stale pre image refusal halts the entire boot
Stale-pre-image refusal halts the entire boot
Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: A mismatching removal record does not only block its own deletion — the value error rises through the replay and the books refuse to open at all.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: One bad removal record in the journal makes every subsequent session unable to start until the journal is repaired.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The stale-pre-image refusal lives inside the replay loop, so its blast radius is the whole journal — the books will not open, all commands that read or write the ledger fail, and only editing or removing the journal line itself (plus possibly a re-fold) clears the block. The message explains what mismatched and refuses loudly, but there is no dedicated tool in the app for repairing a journal line; the repair is a manual, out-of-band act. The care this needs: never edit journal records by hand casually — the same hash-guard machinery that refuses the boot also guards every other row's content.

docs.title: The move to expected hole can leave an entry in neither store
The move-to-expected hole can leave an entry in neither store
Title
docs.text: The move-to-expected hole can leave an entry in neither store

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: The move path deletes the committed entry before creating the planned replacement, so a rejection at the second step destroys the entry with no automatic undo — only a manual rebuild via the expect command.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The one-way deletion-first sequencing of the move needs care — a failed second half loses the entry entirely.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The sequencing choice (delete first, add second) is not transactional: there is no rollback of the deletion when the planned-entry add rejects an amount of zero or a bad value. The recovery is human — the message names the expect command and the bookkeeper must re-enter the values from memory. Care needed: any change to the add/reject path on the expected side, or to zero-amount validation, silently widens this hole. The failure message is the only safety net; a code change that swaps the order, or adds a compensating re-add, removes the exposure.

docs.title: The register strike must never precede a successful commit
The register strike must never precede a successful commit
Title
docs.text: The register strike must never precede a successful commit

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: The delete of the plan row happens only after the confirming booking has applied and returned a committed row; striking first would destroy a plan whose payment never got recorded.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: An ordering-fragile pair — booking then strike — where reversing the order loses the plan permanently, and the code's failure paths all return before the strike.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Confirmation's two writes are ordered deliberately: the books first, the register's strike second, and every refusal path (future date, no amount, booking failure) returns before reaching the strike. Anyone reworking the flow must keep this invariant — a strike that runs before or beside a failed booking would silently retire a plan the books do not reflect, leaving the household with neither plan nor payment. The strike itself is a full-register rewrite, so a crash between booking and strike leaves the plan sitting in the register with its covering commit already on the books — the next confirm or the view's superseding dissolves it, but the registers and books are briefly out of agreement.

docs.title: Transfer edits and moves must keep the savings mirror truthful
Transfer edits and moves must keep the savings mirror truthful
Title
docs.text: Transfer edits and moves must keep the savings mirror truthful

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: Any edit or move of a transfer (Overdracht) touches two account chains — the checking posting and the mirrored savings posting — and the planned register holds only the checking shape, so moves need an explicit savings-side check.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A transfer correction or move re-derives both account chains; the register side has no savings mirror, hence the warnings.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The posting derivation maps a transfer amount onto checking AND its negative onto savings (postings_for). A journaled correction of a transfer therefore re-propagates both chains — right through delete-plus-insert — and the confirmation line shows both balances. But a move of a transfer to the planned register rebuilds the plan through the expected-add route, which books only the checking shape; the savings chain the deletion unwound is not rebuilt as a plan. The code covers this with an explicit warning to check the list view. Care needed: any caller that moves or re-creates transfer rows outside this flow should carry the same warning; a change to postings_for's mirror logic silently changes both chains here.

docs.title: Weekly rule projections depend on an intact start anchor
Weekly rule projections depend on an intact start anchor
Title
docs.text: Weekly rule projections depend on an intact start anchor

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: A weekly or biweekly rule without its start date projects nothing, and its instances' identities derive from the anchor — so editing the anchor reshapes the whole schedule the same rule produces.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The phase anchor is load-bearing: silent no-projection when missing, and every future instance identity changes when the anchor changes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The weekly and biweekly schedule is defined entirely by the rule's start date: expansion walks anchor multiples of seven or fourteen days, and a rule whose anchor is missing (or blank) expands to nothing — the forecast silently shows no weekly instances, with no refusal anywhere, because the blank anchor is only reachable through data edited outside the anchored prompts (the prompts themselves require it; the validation gate refuses saving a weekly rule without one). Related and deliberate: an instance's identity is the content hash of the rule's pattern fields and the occurrence date, so changing the anchor (or description, category, amount) changes every future instance's identity in the forecast. The bookkeeper's stake: an anchor edit is not a cosmetic change — it re-phases the whole schedule and renumbers every due date the rule will ever show.

docs.title: Whole file rule overwrite keeps every writer honest about reload then save
Whole-file rule overwrite keeps every writer honest about reload-then-save
Title
docs.text: Whole-file rule overwrite keeps every writer honest about reload-then-save

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: Every rule mutation reloads the store from disk immediately before rewriting it — a writer that edited an in-memory list from an earlier read would silently erase changes another command made in between.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The store's write shape (rewrite the whole file) makes a stale in-memory rule list the one real corruption risk; the current flow always reloads fresh, and must keep doing so.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The rule store has no per-record updates: every save rewrites the entire file. This is safe only under one discipline, which the current code follows everywhere — load the list, apply the single change, save, with no other read held across user interaction... except the confirmation flows, which do hold the loaded list across the 'ja' prompt (remove) and the seeded loop (add/adopt/edit). The exposure is real but narrow in practice: rules are edited by one bookkeeper in one console, and no other writer shares the store. Any future background writer, sync tool or second console editing the rule file while a prompt is open would land in a lost-update — the earlier load's file would win and the concurrent change would vanish without a message. Anyone touching this flow must keep the load-immediately-before-save shape or introduce a check.

docs.title: subsystems
docs.text:
A thematic grouping of the analyzed system's components — what they jointly deliver — grounded in the analysis's judgment and documented in plain prose.

Fact Sheet Name household bookkeeping stores and corrections household transaction intake

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The grouping of the journaled ledger engine, the expected register store and the cleanup fix engine — the three units that hold the household's recorded books and change them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This grouping covers where the household's financial record lives and how it gets corrected: the journaled ledger engine (the append-only change journal and the ledger it folds into), the expected register store (parked future plans kept apart from the actual books), and the cleanup fix engine (reviewed change-set files applied against the ledger). They form one unit because they share the same data landscape — the data directory's stores and their format conventions — and the same correction discipline: every books change lands through the mutation journal, plans never do, and cleanup is only ever reviewed first. The intake interface and its confirm flow belong to a neighboring grouping focused on capturing entries; this one is the stores-and-corrections side they all write into.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The subsystem by which the household records money movements — quick-add shortcuts, interactive intake, and registering of future plans.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The grouping of everything a recording touches between the bookkeeper's moment of intent and a durable store: the entry interface (prompts, shorthand, validation, dispatch), the register of expected (future) plans, and the journaled ledger engine that applies actual movements with running balances. The components share one business contract — nothing saves without full validation, and what saves is either a balance-carrying actual row or a balance-free planned row.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The intake surface of the product: the household bookkeeper's way to record a movement the moment it happens or is remembered. Three input paths share one validation (a non-empty description, an approved category, a non-zero amount, a date format that parses) and one dispatch: today-or-past dates enter the journaled actual ledger with running balances; a future date diverts the recording to the expected register as a plan. The confirmation echoes the saved entry and its resulting balances. On rejection — invalid detail, zero amount, aborted prompt — nothing is stored and the exit code says so. Ctrl-C is caught and reported as a clean cancellation with nothing saved.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
edit — correct a recorded transaction or a planned entry.

Run with an id from the list view ('financials list') to edit that one entry, or bare to pick from the last ten actual rows. The editor shows the current row first and then asks for date, description, category and amount in one pass — pressing Enter keeps each current value. For a committed row the finished correction is journaled as a full replacement; the console line reports the updated entry together with the new checking and savings balances. Editing a committed row to a future date instead moves it out of the committed ledger into the planned-entry register (date, description, category and amount carried over). For a planned entry, an edit toward today or the past confirms the entry into the ledger as it now stands; an edit that keeps it in the future rewrites the plan where it sits. Ids that belong to a group or a recurring-entry instance are handed to their own editors (group editor, occurrence editor).

    console.print("[dim]Niets openstaand om te bevestigen.[/dim]")
    return None
  table = Table(title="Openstaand (geland maar niet bevestigd)", box=box.SIMPLE)
  columns: list[tuple[str, Literal["left", "right"]]] = [
    ("Id", "left"),
    ("Datum", "left"),
    ("Omschrijving", "left"),
    ("Categorie", "left"),
    ("Bedrag", "right"),
  ]
  for column, justify in columns:
    table.add_column(column, justify=justify)
  for t in rows:
    table.add_row(t.id, t.date, t.description, t.category, f"{t.amount_eur:+,.2f}")
  console.print(table)
  text = Prompt.ask("Id om te bevestigen (leeg = annuleren)", default="")
  return text.strip() or None
